checked_sound: att/att_it/att_i/att_itime weights (ado:2178-2209) match the help: w/W_it by (i,t); w/W_ipost or w/W_ipre via the posttreatment classification (reported pre cells only, so the reference period and, under timetrends, the extra normalized period drop out of W_ipre through _t = 0); w/(W_it*T_i) with T_i counting periods cohort i is observed, by (posttreatment, i).
customweightmultiplier() multiplies the margins weights only, not the regression weights (ado:815, 2131); under att_it it enters the numerator only, which matches 'multiplied'.

Estimand table (guide:170-175) and 'Invalid Estimands' (sthlp:629-632): att_it at a single horizon weights cohorts equally by construction of w_att_it; att_i/att_itime horizons are reported as att_it.
gteffects: weighted means under all four weight columns reproduce the main and pretreatment rows exactly, and under w_att and w_att_it the event-study rows (probe p3).
IM claim that att equals att_i with cluster at the cohort level follows from equal cluster weighting.
anticipation(): the shift is applied once to ttre before _t is built (ado:1007-1008), and the oostreatedcontrols window reads the shifted onset; equals manual ttre-# exactly (memory benchmarks).
Out-of-window onsets are treated as never-treated by default (ado:1008), as sthlp:204 says.
The requirement of a never-treated or post-window cohort is enforced: dta_path_nonever refused under both reference regimes (probe p7, rc 459).
hdidregress twfe equality with wooldid default, i = onset cohort, no controls: 1.925584 on both (probe p4); Stata notes notyet equals never for twfe when never-treated exist.
did_imputation equals wooldid at i = unit on an unbalanced panel (1.85877 both) and at any i on a balanced one (probe p6), apart from the omission filed as F3.
interactivecontrols(): demeaned by i with regression weights, slope keyed on 1.targetflag, reported as part of the effect; location-invariant (probe p1: 1.9245 at x and x+100).
controls(): pooled slope, standard; with a fine i coefficients come from untreated rows only, as the did_imputation paragraph says.

Cell collapse: key (_i,_t,targetflag,ifvar,t,ttre,subgroups, plus cluster under impvalues and i/lattice/cfxlattice under contreat) and the ineligible list in validate (~5872-5917) match sthlp:288-297 and guide:252-254; binary and poisson xb differences are cell-constant so collapsed margins are exact.
Poisson effects on the linear-index (log) scale: RULED (review_process/open_ticket_poisexp_dydx_2026-09-19.md, level-scale results removed 2026-09-20).
Subgroup rules: a cohort must lie wholly in one subgroup because subgroups only reweight cell effects; share weighting under safety(off) changes att_i/att_itime as documented.
Triple-diff regression (group by period fixed effects with i split by group) is the right model; the defect filed as F4 is in the aggregation.
Description of Z and the fixed-reference saturation (sthlp:164-169) is accurate.
bootdf() default is clusters when cluster() is given and normal otherwise (ado 562), and G counts the estimation-sample clusters (wdb_r_nclus). This matches help L381-387 and guide L299.

Percentile interval uses the classic Stata order-statistic rule (ado 17694-17699). Percentile p = min(1, 2 min(m0,m1)/n) with weak inequalities is the exact inversion of that interval, floor 2/n, and can be 0 (ado 17726-17728). This matches help L373 and guide L349.

BC: z0 = invnormal(#(draws <= comparator)/n) is Stata's convention. The endpoints Phi(2 z0 + z_alpha) are right, and the p-value q = Phi(Phi^-1(r0) - 2 z0), p = 2 min(q, 1-q), correctly inverts the BC interval (ado 17729-17749). This matches the formula in guide L301/L351. The BC convention is ruled.

BCa: the acceleration a = sum(mean - theta_g)^3 / (6 [sum(mean - theta_g)^2]^1.5) from a delete-one-cluster jackknife is Efron (1987) with the correct sign. The endpoint map and the p inversion zr/(1 + a zr) - z0 are algebraically correct (ado 17802-17855). Requiring cluster() for bca is sound.

boottstat: t_r = (b_r - b)/se_r against t_obs = b/se_obs. The equal-tailed percentile-t interval [b - q_hi se, b - q_lo se] is Hall's construction. The add-one p 2(1+min)/(n+1) has floor 2/(n+1) and cannot be 0 (ado 16224-16292), matching help L374/L398-400 and guide L295-297. The add-one convention is ruled (F033).
Refusing bootdisplay(bc)/bca under boottstat, and boottstat under poisson and bayes, is a ruled design choice with a sound rationale: a replication se must be the same functional of the resample.

The frequency-weight studentization defect is described correctly: the expected ratio of mean-square replication se to observed se is E[m^2] = 2 - 1/G (guide L283). Physical re-identification for boottstat with cluster() is the correct fix.
Fixed-metric bootstrap joint tests W_r = (b_r - b)' Sigma^-1 (b_r - b) on the listwise bootstrap covariance, one-sided add-one with floor 1/(n+1) (ado 18370-18414), match help L374 and guide L357.

e(V) under bootstrap is the listwise replication covariance rescaled to the per-column bootstrap sd, a congruence transform that preserves PSD and correlations (ado 16566-16604). The reported bootstrap se is the sd of the draws (n-1 divisor). This matches help L393 and L1129.
The reps() resolution caution thresholds (2/(reps+1) under boottstat, 1/(reps+1) under wald, 2/reps otherwise, ado 7469-7473) match help L372-374 and guide L285.

Bayesian bootstrap draws Gamma(1) per cluster, normalized, applied as a per-row multiplier (equal). bootalpha(size) draws Gamma(n_c) and divides by n_c (ado 16171-16209). This matches help L376-379 and guide L293. The claim that size shrinks the weight dispersion by roughly sqrt(mean cluster size) is right.
The refusal of bayes with the cell-weighted estimands (the cell-sampling component is omitted) is ruled and econometrically sound.

IM: per-cluster margins over(cluster) with nose, ttest against 0, t(q-1) row by row, e(df_r) set to the minimum q-1 (ado 2594-2669, 4876), CI b +/- invt(q-1) se. This matches help L271-279 and guide L226. Refusing a cluster finer than i is sound: the per-cluster reads are re-weightings of shared coefficients (blue-sky oob-impvalues measured se ratio sqrt((K-1)/(nK-1))). The independence caveat about shared controls is correctly qualified (help L340-346, guide L311).

Analytic att rows under cluster() at or above i are understated without a caution (help L315, guide L200). Probe p1 confirmed .158 against a Monte Carlo sd of .257. The att row under bootstrap(standard) is valid there (.249 against .257).
Guide L220 degrees-of-freedom note: reghdfe drops fixed effects nested in the cluster from K and regress with explicit dummies does not, so the regress path is conservative. Correct.
unconditionalse requires a robust-type first stage (robust, cluster, a robust customvce, or pweights), as margins vce(unconditional) needs. The subpopulation remark (help L327-329) is correct.
customvce() refuses bootstrap and impvalues, and the regress path cannot absorb fe(). Described correctly.
level() domain 10-99.99 is validated in the code (ado 7209). pretrendpower's pre-test size is fixed at 5%.

simultaneousbands: the analytic sup-t band uses a common sqrt(chi2(df)/df) divisor, a multivariate t with the pointwise df. The bootstrap band uses the level() quantile of the max studentized deviation. Both are sound. No floor at the pointwise quantile is a ruled choice.
Excluding failed replications and counting them in e(boot_failed) follows Stata's bootstrap convention, disclosed in help L371 and in the few-treated caution.
The guide's warning that the posted analytic e(V) has zero off-diagonals across families, so cross-family tests on it are invalid (help L1124-1127, guide pitfall 21), is correct.

Equal-tailed p = min(1, 2 min(P_lo, P_hi)) with add-one (1+m)/(n+1) for sampled draws and plain shares when the observed assignment is in the reference set: matches wooldid_permtail/permmemb exactly. The Phipson-Smyth justification is right for draws with replacement, including under permute(probabilities), where the observed assignment and the draws are iid from the design.

Floors: 2/(n+1) by default and 1/(n+1) under permabsp/permside; 2/M and 1/M exact; 0 possible under permrawp. The worked numbers are right (50->.039, 100->.020, 199->.010, 999->.002; one treated cluster among 12 gives .167/.083). The 'below 39' threshold is consistent with reject-at-p<=.05.

Shift interval [b - q_hi, b - q_lo] with q at (100-level)/200 and 1-(100-level)/200 by the bootci order-statistic rule. Scaled by se_obs under permtstat. Exact dual of the equal-tailed test up to add-one (an MC agent verified this at permreps(79)).
permabsp interval b +/- the level/100 quantile of |s_r| is the dual of the absolute-value p. permside keeps the two-sided interval. permrawp is ritest's c/n share.
Off-centre guard: when the signed central band excludes 0 the shift interval cannot contain the estimate. Blanking the interval and keeping the p is correct.

Exact enumeration: distinct multiset permutations per stratum, crossed across strata, are equally likely under a uniform shuffle. The plain share with the observed assignment included is exact. An incompletely enumerated element keeps an exact share over the completed assignments, which is valid because estimability is a function of the assignment alone.

Excluding failed replications is valid for the sharp null: estimability depends only on the assignment, and the observed assignment is estimable, so conditioning on estimability preserves exchangeability. The same holds for the ame structural-zero exclusion and for per-element counts in e(perm_n).

Joint, equality and adversarial quadratic forms use a metric computed symmetrically from all draws plus the comparator (the comparator is appended only when it is not already a member), so W_obs and the W_r are exchangeable and the one-sided add-one p is valid. The same holds for the listwise-complete step-down.

Step-down algorithm: studentization by the null-draw SD, ordering by |t_obs|, max over the not-yet-rejected horizons, and monotonization are all standard. p_raw is in the step-down's own metric, as documented.
e(perm_p_se) = mult*sqrt(q(1-q)/n) on the underlying share, with Clopper-Pearson doubled under the equal-tailed rule. Both are missing under exact enumeration. This matches the text.
The shift interval widens with the true effect and is calibrated only near the null: confirmed by F058 s6.7 and by my probe (default width .77 -> 2.89 at tau 0 -> 5).

permtstat removes the growth for the post-treatment rows (help:498, footer ado:13179): confirmed by probe3 with i = cohort, cluster(state), fe(state) and permonsetcohorts. The permtstat main_att width was .703/.713 at tau 0 against .688/.727 at tau 5. The contrasts are never studentized, so 'not for the contrasts' is right.

The pre-treatment caveat is right: in staggered designs reassigned onsets move post-treatment outcomes into the draws' pre horizons, so pre p-values rise toward 1. The single-onset exception is also right, because the pre horizons are calendar periods before any unit is treated, so the effect never enters them.

Recoding onsets after the last period to never-treated leaves the shuffle p-values unchanged: labels that the estimator reads identically are merged, which marginalizes over estimation-equivalent assignments.

permprobs zero-probability caution: correctly says the p is a tail probability under the design, not a randomization test containing the observed assignment. The possible-assignment count is the product of support sizes.

Subgroup contrasts and the equality tests test the sharp null, not equality (the labelling is right; see PERM-6 for the direction sub-clause). The shuffle without permstrata re-randomizes subgroup composition, as the caution says.

Randomization inference produces a null distribution, not a sampling covariance, so refusing pretrendpower() and not posting a permutation e(V) are right. The shift SE is not a sampling SE, as the text says.
permtci: b +/- the level quantile of |t_r| times se_obs. It coincides with the table interval under permtstat+permabsp, as stated.
Assignment unit and nesting: one onset per cluster needs a cluster that nests i. permonsetcohorts rebuilding i from the drawn onsets is a well-defined map under the checked bijection.
gteffects cells and the assignment-keyed lattice types have no permutation distribution because their keys move with the assignment. Blanking them is right.

Regression form (help 188, 777): cell intercepts plus cell-by-f(dose) slopes plus g(f(dose)); code i._i#i._t#i.targetflag##[i.lat##]c.dose with a bit-exact double 'ringer' copy in absorb() partialling out the baseline slope, so the pooled visible c.dose is dropped (ado 1360-1376, 1482-1539).

ame = cell slope net of the g() reference slope (help 800-804), via margins dydx(contreat) on treated rows; the att = beta_it + delta_it*dose via dydx(targetflag); under untreatedZero the ame is the total within-cell slope (g = 0), as help 811-813 says.

contreatcontrols types map to the documented interactions (basic: i.null##ringer, with a lattice also i.lat##ringer; byTreated/byTtre/byCohort/byTime: group#[lat#]ringer plus group##lat intercepts); byTime alongside another type is additive, as help 808 says.
byTime refused under contreatwithin (help 818-819): with no untreated rows in a period, the period slope absorbs the treated slope; that reasoning is correct.

Reference-pool screen (help 766-769, guide rule 1): sd of the dose over tcell==0 rows per group, refused at or below 1e-5 of the sample sd or with fewer than 2 rows, caution between that and 1e-3; byCohort screen unconditional; byTime fails after the last onset when never-treated doses are zero or constant. The code matches, and the band was ruled 2026-09-23.
Probe p6: a lattice whose upper bins have no reference-row support, with a homogeneous baseline slope, gives correct ame and bin att (1.00, and 1.55/2.58/3.55 against truth 1.5/2.5/3.5).

Cell containment (help 821-826, guide 649): with every treated cell inside one cluster, the cell-specific scores sum to zero within the cluster, so the ame sandwich variance collapses to the baseline-slope variance (basic) or zero (untreatedZero). Reporting it as missing is correct, single-row cells are exempt, and bootstrap, permute, impvalues and robust (independent errors) are valid alternatives.

contreatelasticitytype: dydx(xb) under poisson is the semi-elasticity of E[y] and dyex(xb) the elasticity (help 687); Stata's semi-elasticity labelling of dyex on the linear path is Stata's own convention. Note: margins dyex is x*dy/dx for any sign of x (probe p5), so the proportional-change reading needs a positive dose on treated rows; the guide's poisson centring note (guide 83) correctly says a centred dose changes what dyex means.

Cell collapse under a dose (guide 232, 252-254; help 288-296): exact because att, ame and dyex are linear in the dose within a cell (bin), with the lattice and cfxlattice bins in the key; contreatpoly > 1 and the dose inside controls/fe/ccc_absorb are correctly listed as ineligible.

Lattice construction (help 697-721): generated bins by gquantiles xtile within the documented by-groups; the baseTreated* types use treated-group cutpoints applied everywhere (baseTreatedRef uses _t==0 pre-onset rows; baseTreatedPre all pre-onset rows); weights used unless latticeignoreweights; under bootstrap the resample multiplicity is kept, so each replication re-forms its bins (a correct bootstrap of an estimated-quantile procedure).

Lattice interpretation (help 781-786): the lattice adds within-cell intercepts that the ame does not capture, so the ame and the att can disagree; reading the att where the intercepts carry the effect is sound advice.

makecfxplots restricted to att (help 713-716, guide 193): under att_it/att_i weights a bin that cuts across cells or cohorts no longer gives equal cell or cohort weight, so the restriction is econometrically justified.

ccc_absorb (help 889-895): i._i#i._t#c.(vars) absorbed, the same model as coarsecohortcontrols for continuous variables; a variable constant within cells is collinear with the cell dummy, as stated. ccnoabsorb moves the same set into explicit regressors, the same model (ado 1592-1599).
contreatwithin with i-by-t effects in fe(): every intercept is absorbed and the att equals mean(delta*dose); correct in that special case only (see CT-3).

permute with contreat (guide 383): the dose stays with the unit and only timing is permuted; untreatedZero refused because reassigned onset contradicts its zero-dose premise; assignment-dependent lattice types blanked. Coherent.

Caution on putting the dose in controls() (help 862-865): a renamed copy is harmless, and under untreatedZero such a control is collinear with the cell slopes, so the recommendation to avoid untreatedZero there is correct.

pretrendpower() slope: GLS through the reference, slope = m'S^-1 b / m'S^-1 m with m = relyr - esrelativeto built from the actual labels (both signs under esrelativeto < -1), se = 1/sqrt(m'S^-1 m); interval at level() with t(df_r) where df exists (ado 11800-11990).

mdt_wald = sqrt(lambda / m'S^-1 m), with lambda the noncentrality from npnF(k, df_r, invF(k, df_r, .95), 1 - power), or chi2 without df. This is the right noncentral-F power inversion for the joint Wald pre-test at 5%.

bias columns = mdt x (hbar - reference): correct for the fixed-base pooled estimand under a linear trend gamma(h - ref). hbar is estimand-weighted over the FULL post support (not the window), att_it-family weights for att_it/ame_it, and is correctly documented as the unconditional bias 'if it continued'.

mdt_nis / NIS size: 1 - P(all |b_j| < 1.96 sd_j) under the normal law with the full pre-period covariance (mvnormalcvqp), at 5% and independent of level(), with the bisection on exact power. This matches Roth's pretrends convention, and the help states the normal reference and the 4-pre-period cap correctly.

pretrendpower() refusals (impvalues, fastnose, permute; requires esfixedbaseperiod and espre >= 1) and the cluster-at-or-above-i caution shared with jointtests (ado 1872-1920) match the help and the guide table.

jointtests thresholds: two pre horizons in the window, three under esfixedbaseperiod + timetrends at esrelativeto(-1) (ado 2858 condition), the test over the requested window, and the caution under analytic clustering at or above i. Under bootstrap without boottstat it is the recentred fixed-metric rank test (ado 7823-7880); under permute it is a permutation test of the sharp null. All as documented.

esfixedbaseperiod pretreatment row averages every estimable pre-period except the reference (margins subpop t < ttre & _t != 0, ado 2683), while the joint test uses the window. Correctly documented at sthlp 544 and guide 437.

Pooled reference: every pre-period before the requested window, plus each unit's first observed period, forms the reference (wooldid_reltime). The main row pools every post cell whatever espostlength. The did_imputation equivalence needs esprelength(0) because requested pre horizons leave the reference and move the post estimates. All correct.

Adversarial null under esfixedbaseperiod: b_h = c(h - esrelativeto), one free parameter, q = rank(V) - 1, F(q, df_r) or chi2. Under timetrends it collapses to b = 0 with q = rank(V) (ado 16030-16055). Help and guide state this correctly.

altmethod_adversarial: forecast error b_Q - A b_P tested against V_QQ + A V_PP A' - A V_PQ - V_PQ' A' (ado 16063-16095). The covariance algebra is right and needs one real pre coefficient beyond the reference, as documented.

Adversarial display line e(adversarial_line_*) is an unweighted free-intercept OLS including the planted zero reference row, which is not the tested one-parameter null. The help describes it faithfully, and research_2026-09-08/adversarial_null.md records 'the sweep says leave it', so it is a ruled design choice and not filed.

Analytic sup-t band: correlation matrix from e(V_es_*), max|z| over the family's horizons, a common sqrt(chi2_df/df) divisor giving the multivariate-t sup quantile at df_r, no floor at the pointwise quantile (ruled). The bootstrap band is the max-|t| over listwise-complete replications, percentile-t under boottstat. Construction is correct (Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Moller 2019).

honestdid handoff conditions: esfixedbaseperiod at esrelativeto(-1), no timetrends, at least one pre and one post, consecutive horizons, no degenerate rows. e(b_es_*) columns are chronological with the reference omitted, and e(numpre_*) counts pre columns, which is what honestdid's positional geometry needs.

anticipation(#) is equivalent to ttre - # applied before relative time is built (did_imputation shift()). Horizons count from the effective onset; esfixedbaseperiod drops units whose shifted reference is unusable. As documented.

Permutation pre-period caveat: pre-treatment p-values, including the joint and adversarial tests, test the sharp null of no effect at any horizon and rise toward 1 with the true effect in staggered designs. Stated at sthlp 497-501 and guide 374.
Invalid estimands: at a single relative period att_i, att_itime and att_it coincide (one cell per i per horizon), so only the att and att_it event studies are shown. Correct.
Guide pitfall 6 and ch4 rule 2: adversarial p-values at cluster at or above i are oversized and not cautioned. That matches the code: the caution gate covers jointtests and pretrendpower only.

Every poisson margins call uses predict(xb) (ado:2440-2445), on the ppmlhdfe path and on the Stata-poisson path under unconditionalse/customvce(). Effects are differences or derivatives of the linear index, so the absorbed effects d cancel and the delta-method Jacobian is complete (open_ticket_poisexp_dydx: the truncated-Jacobian defect was reachable only through the removed poisexpresults).

Under poisson, dydx on xb is the semi-elasticity d ln E[y]/dc and dyex is the elasticity d ln E[y]/d ln c (help :686, guide :523, ado:2530 labels). The linear-path dyex is correctly titled a semi-elasticity (dy/d ln c). The guide's 'xb = ln E[y|x]' omits ppmlhdfe's absorbed d, which is harmless because only differences and derivatives are reported.

The dyex centring note (help :535, guide :83) is right. Centring the dose leaves dydx slopes and the att unchanged (cell intercepts absorb the shift) but changes dyex, which scales by the centred dose.

The ame under poisson is the average over treated cells of the cell dose slope on ln E[y], net of the baseline g() slope carried by the ringer that margins does not toggle. It is consistently described as a semi-elasticity or elasticity of E[y].

'Parallel trends in proportions' (help :528, guide :83 'one group is always 2x the other') is the ratio parallel-trends assumption of the exponential-mean DiD (Wooldridge 2023). The log(y)-with-zeros motivation does not claim equivalence with E[ln y].

Perfect separation (help :536, guide :83): an all-zero treated cell drives its cell dummy to minus infinity, and naming it as separation rather than collinearity is correct. Under safety(off), excluding it changes the realized sample, which the guide states.

The r(3200) retry fits the same model. Absorbed and explicit terms span the same columns, the retry keeps fe() absorbed, and the explicit ringer-first order is deliberate. The r(3201) handling enters the dose polynomial explicitly (same as ccnoabsorb) and splits ccc_absorb() into one slope per factor copy, which is the same column space (ado:1600-1660).
Plain contreatcontrols(basic) under poisson enters the pooled dose control, and ccc_absorb() with it, explicitly (ado:1603-1609), with the ccnoabsorb carve-out, as help :530-532 says.

The dropped-pooled-dose-control caution (help :534-535) is correct: ppmlhdfe's collinearity tolerance is relative to the raw uncentred sum of squares (ado:2000-2005 comment), so a large-mean, small-spread dose trips it, and centring avoids it.
jointmarginsdof under poisson passes df(.), so joint tests are chi-squared Wald tests. Under unconditionalse it adds vce(unconditional). This agrees with the z columns (probe p1).

Poisson and regress paths compared (probe p2): poisson cluster(unit) fe(unit) through ppmlhdfe and poisson customvce(cluster unit) controls(i.unit) through Stata's poisson give the same att and SEs to 4e-11. So the nested-FE degrees-of-freedom divergence at guide :220 is a regress-path statement and does not arise under poisson. The linear pair does diverge as documented (.3438 vs .3672).

Pseudo-R2: e(r2pseud) is ppmlhdfe's e(r2_p) = 1 - ll/ll_0, and ppmlhdfe's ll_0 is the intercept-only log-likelihood (ppmlhdfe.mata:445-449, although ppmlhdfe.sthlp:279 says fixed-effects-only). That is the same baseline as Stata poisson's, so the statistic is comparable across the two poisson paths. The ado spells vce(cluster) so Stata's poisson posts ll_0 and r2_p (ado:1960-1966). e(chi2) is passed through as the estimator's Wald statistic, as help :1067 says.

unconditionalse under poisson: margins vce(unconditional) after poisson with robust, cluster or pweight is valid linearization. The parse gate (ado:5492) enforces the robust/cluster/pweight requirement the help states.
customvce() under poisson passes the text to Stata's poisson and makes no claim about equidispersion. A customvce(oim) run is correctly labelled oim by its first word.
Probe p1 shows the pseudo-R2 unchanged between the robust and no-vce runs, and the z label under poisson on both.

findings_all.quote: reported treatment effects will not vary as a direct function of these controls; the effect of these controls are partialled out from the reported treatment effects.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: coarsecohortcontrols() is built at ado:1397 as i._i#i._t#(vars): every treated cell gets its own control slope, and the (0,0) reference cell slope acts as the pooled slope. The term is not keyed on targetflag, and margins toggles only targetflag, so the treated cell's own slope stays in the counterfactual. The reported cell effect is therefore beta_it, the treated-cell intercept at control value 0 (for a factor control, the effect in the base category), not the cell ATT beta_it + xbar_it*(s_it - s_ref). The estimate moves when a constant is added to the control. Probe p1 (tau = 1 + .5(x-5) + 2g, true ATT 2.00, i = onset cohort, fe(unit)): coarse(c.x) -0.526, coarse(c.x+100) -49.40, coarse(c.x-5) 1.92, coarse(i.g) 0.97 (the g=0 effect), interactivecontrols(x) 1.92 at both x and x+100, controls(x) 1.94. Probe p2 (constant effect 1.5): coarse(c.x) 1.435 vs coarse(c.x+100) 1.747, so even under homogeneous effects the estimate is an extrapolation to x=0 with noise scaling in |xbar|. The same defect makes the BJS paragraph (sthlp:1160-1165, 'closer to the spirit of BJS') and example 3 (sthlp:1186-1188) misleading, and guide:614 and guide:641 repeat 'partialled out'.
findings_all.correct_statement: With cell-specific control slopes and a pooled slope estimated on untreated rows, the cell effect under an imputation counterfactual is beta_it + xbar_it*(s_it - s_ref), the average over the cell of the fitted outcome minus the fitted outcome at the pooled slope. That quantity is invariant to shifting the control by a constant. Reference: Wooldridge (2025, Empirical Economics), covariates enter the cohort-by-time interactions centred at cohort means so that the dummy coefficient is ATT(g,t); Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024, Review of Economic Studies), Y(0) imputed with covariate coefficients from untreated observations; the general result that the coefficient on a dummy interacted with an uncentred covariate is the effect at covariate = 0 (Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, ch. 6.2).
findings_all.proposed_fix: Code, ado:1397 (and the same fix serves ccc_absorb, F1b): enter the controls once as pooled regressors, and give each treated cell a slope on the control centred at its weighted cell mean, built on a copy that is 0 on reference rows: regressors (vars) plus i._i#i._t#c.(vars_cellcentred). The column space is unchanged, so the fit is unchanged, but the cell intercept becomes ybar_it minus the fitted Y(0) at the pooled slope, which is the cell ATT; margins still reads it by toggling targetflag, the effect stays constant within the cell (cell collapse stays exact, gteffects' 'reproduces exactly' stays true). For factor controls centre each indicator column within the cell, or use the alternative spelling (vars) plus i._i#i._t#1.targetflag#(vars) (same column space; margins then removes intercept and slope together, but the effect then varies within the cell, so coarsecohortcontrols must join fcbad at validate ~5872 and gteffects must add the slope term). Help, replace sthlp:845-850 with: {phang}{opt coarse:cohortcontrols()}: Includes the specified controls, and interactions between them and every Tz_it dummy in the model, one per cohort-time period for which a treatment effect is estimated (under {it:esfixedbaseperiod}, every estimable treated cohort by relative time period). The control slopes in the reference period and the control group are pooled, while each treated cohort-period gets its own slope. Each reported effect is the cell's average outcome less its predicted untreated outcome at the pooled slope, so it does not depend on where the control is centred. All coarse cohort controls must use factor notation, {it:c.} for continuous and {it:i.} for categorical. {p_end}. Guide:614 and 616, third column: 'partialled out at the pooled slope; the effect is the cell average'. Until the code is fixed, the help must say the reported effect is the treated-cell intercept at a control value of zero and that controls must be centred on their treated cell means.

findings_all.quote: The difference in SG level estimates returned will be the triple diff estimate.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: A triple difference removes shocks that hit both groups in a treated cohort and period only when the two group-level DiDs average the same cohort-by-period cells with the same weights. Under the default att each subgroup weights its cells by its own observation counts, so the contrast is sum_c w1_c*delta_c + sum_c (w1_c - w0_c)*s_c and the shared shock s_c survives whenever group shares differ across cohorts or periods. Probe p5 (onset 4 has 80% g=1, onset 6 has 20%, shared cohort-period shock +2/-2 on both groups, true DDD 1, i = group(ttre g), fe(i.unit i.g##i.t) subgroups(g)): att contrast 3.97 (se .17); att_it contrast 1.14 (se .22). The guide's recipe (guide:1355) uses att and guide:480 and guide:500 repeat the claim.
findings_all.correct_statement: With i defined as onset cohort by group and both groups present in every treated cohort-by-period cell, the att_it contrast is the equally weighted mean of the cell-level triple differences and removes cohort-by-period shocks common to the two groups. The att contrast does so only if the group shares are the same in every cell. Olden and Moen (2022), 'The triple difference estimator', Econometrics Journal 25(3); Ortiz-Villavicencio and Sant'Anna (2025), 'Better Understanding Triple Differences Estimators' (working paper), on DDD not being a plain difference of two DiDs under staggered adoption.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Replace sthlp:671-674 with: {pstd} A special case is the triple difference. All cohorts fall into two groups, and both groups appear among the treated and the control cohorts. Define {it:i} as the treatment onset cohort by group, specify the group as the SG variable, and add group by period fixed effects, as in {it:subgroups(sgvarname) fe(i.sgvarname##i.t)}. The contrast removes shocks shared by the two groups in a treated cohort and period only when both subgroup estimates average the same cohort-by-period cells with the same weights. Use {it:att_it}, with both groups present in every treated cohort-by-period cell; its contrast is then the simple average of the cell-level triple differences. The {it:att} contrast weights each group's cells by its own observation counts, so it keeps those shocks whenever the group shares differ across cells. {p_end}. Guide:480: 'A triple difference is subgroups(g) fe(i.g##i.t) with att_it and i defined as onset cohort by group; the att_it contrast is the triple-difference estimate when both groups are present in every treated cell. The att contrast is not.' Guide:1355: change att to att_it.
findings_all.reference: Olden and Moen (2022) Econometrics Journal; Ortiz-Villavicencio and Sant'Anna (2025)
findings_all.ruling_checked: Grepped review_process/ for triple|DDD: only unrelated hits (blue_sky structure_and_ux 'p-value convention triple'). No ruling.

findings_all.quote: If the user specifies the option {it:esfixedbaseperiod}, {it:wooldid} will switch to employing a fixed reference period, meaning that all treatment effect estimates will be formed by comparing treated cohorts' average outcomes
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The 'Two Approaches' discussion (sthlp:610-627, guide:417 and 465-469) presents the choice as a transparency versus precision tradeoff over the reference period only. It also changes the comparison group and the identifying assumption. Under the default every untreated row identifies the period effects, including not-yet-treated cohorts' pre-treatment rows (the imputation estimator). Under esfixedbaseperiod every treated-cohort pre-period cell except the reference carries its own dummy, so the period effects come from never-treated cohorts, cohorts treated after the window, and each treated cohort's single reference row; not-yet-treated cohorts stop serving as controls. Probe p3: adding 5t to a not-yet-treated cohort's early pre-period outcomes moved the default att 1.8456 -> 1.895 and left the esfixedbaseperiod att at 1.67445 exactly. Neither the help nor the guide says this anywhere.
findings_all.correct_statement: The default (pooled reference) uses never-treated, post-window and not-yet-treated observations as controls and requires parallel trends and no anticipation across all untreated periods (Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess 2024; Wooldridge 2025). The fixed reference uses never-treated and post-window cohorts plus each treated cohort's reference row, and requires parallel trends relative to those cohorts from the reference period on (the never-treated comparison of Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021 and Sun and Abraham 2021).
findings_all.proposed_fix: Add after sthlp:615: {pstd} The choice also changes the comparison group. Under the pooled reference period every untreated observation serves as a control: never-treated cohorts, cohorts treated after the sample, and the pre-treatment periods of cohorts not yet treated. Parallel trends must then hold across all of those periods. Under {it:esfixedbaseperiod} each treated cohort's pre-treatment periods other than the reference period carry their own indicators, so the period effects are estimated from never-treated cohorts, cohorts treated after the sample, and each treated cohort's reference period. Not-yet-treated cohorts then do not serve as controls, and parallel trends is needed only relative to the never-treated cohorts from the reference period on. {p_end}. Add the same two sentences to the guide's pooled-or-fixed decision rule at guide:417.
findings_all.reference: Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024) REStud; Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) J. Econometrics; Sun and Abraham (2021) J. Econometrics
findings_all.ruling_checked: Grepped review_process/ for never.treated|not.yet|comparison group with esfixedbaseperiod; no ruling. Probe p7 on test/data/dta_path_nonever.dta: both reference regimes refuse (rc 459) without a never-treated or post-window cohort, so the design does not collapse silently; severity kept at medium.

findings_all.quote: {it:did_imputation} given that one uses the {it:att} estimand-type, uses a pooled reference period (i.e., not using {it:esfixedbaseperiod}), requests no
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The equivalence conditions omit the level of i. did_imputation uses unit fixed effects; wooldid uses cohort effects on i. On an unbalanced panel with a coarse i they differ, with or without fe(unit). Probe p3 (unbalanced, no controls): BJS 1.85877, wooldid i=unit 1.85877 (equal), i=onset cohort 1.92558, i=onset cohort with fe(unit) 1.84560. Probe p6 (same DGP, balanced): all four equal 2.04396979. The guide's comparison table (guide:1314) has the same omission.
findings_all.correct_statement: The point estimates coincide when i is the unit, or when the panel is balanced within each i (Wooldridge 2025's pooled-cohort and TWFE equivalence is a balanced-panel result).
findings_all.proposed_fix: Replace sthlp:1153-1155 wording with: For binary treatments, {it:wooldid} will yield the same estimates as {it:did_imputation} given that one uses the {it:att} estimand-type, uses a pooled reference period (i.e., not using {it:esfixedbaseperiod}), requests no pre-treatment horizons ({it:esprelength(0)}), does not use unconditional standard errors, does not use controls, and either defines {it:i} at the unit level or has a panel balanced within each {it:i}. On an unbalanced panel with a coarse {it:i} the two differ, with or without unit fixed effects in {it:fe()}. Guide:1314 second column: add 'i at the unit level or a panel balanced within i'.

findings_all.quote: fixed effects in {opt fe()}, which a coarse {it:i} also needs when the panel is unbalanced within cohorts.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The advice is right that fe(unit) removes the composition bias from permanent unit differences, but the help and guide:103 ('holds the point estimate fixed') imply it restores the observation-weighted estimate. With unit fixed effects, a coarse cell's coefficient weights its units by the within-unit variance of the treatment dummy (T_j p_j(1-p_j)), not by their treated rows; a unit with no untreated rows contributes nothing to its cell coefficient while its rows still carry att weight. With unit-level effect heterogeneity it matches the unit-level estimate only on balanced panels. Probe p3 (unbalanced, effects vary with the unit effect): i=unit 1.8588, coarse i + fe(unit) 1.8456, coarse i without fe 1.9256; p6 balanced: all equal.
findings_all.correct_statement: On an unbalanced panel, coarse i with unit fixed effects gives a variance-weighted average of unit effects within each cell; it equals the observation-weighted (unit-level i) estimate when effects are homogeneous within cells or the panel is balanced. Angrist (1998) Econometrica; Gibbons, Suarez Serrato and Urbancic (2019), 'Broken or Fixed Effects?', Journal of Econometric Methods.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Append to sthlp:69 before {p_end}: On such a panel the unit fixed effects remove bias from permanent differences between units, but each cell's estimate then weights its units by how their rows split between untreated and treated periods. Where treatment effects differ across the units of a cohort, define {it:i} at the unit level if the observation weighting matters. Guide:103: add the same two sentences.
findings_all.reference: Angrist (1998); Gibbons, Suarez Serrato and Urbancic (2019)
findings_all.ruling_checked: Grepped review_process/ for 'unbalanced', 'fe(unit)', 'finest-i': rulings concern runtime and clustering (wooldid-fineclus tickets), none on the within-cell weighting.

findings_all.quote:
use of a pooled reference period is likely disadvantageous whenever the outcome variable
is evolving over time within the pre-treatment period.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: Common evolution of the outcome is absorbed by the period effects and does not disadvantage the pooled reference. The disadvantage arises when treated cohorts' outcomes evolve differently from the comparison group's (a parallel-trends violation), where a fixed reference at -1 limits the bias at short horizons. guide:417 ('when the outcome trends within the pre-period') and guide:469 repeat it.
findings_all.correct_statement: The pooled reference is disadvantageous when treated cohorts trend differently from the comparison units before treatment; common trends are absorbed by the time effects. Roth, Sant'Anna, Bilinski and Poe (2023), J. Econometrics, survey section on pre-trends and reference periods.
findings_all.proposed_fix: sthlp:622-623: 'use of a pooled reference period is likely disadvantageous whenever the outcomes of treated cohorts evolve differently from those of the comparison cohorts within the pre-treatment period.' guide:417: 'Prefer the fixed reference when treated cohorts' outcomes trend differently from the comparison group's in the pre-period'. guide:469: as the help.
findings_all.reference: Roth, Sant'Anna, Bilinski and Poe (2023)
findings_all.ruling_checked: Grepped review_process/ for 'pooled reference' and 'evolving': no ruling on this sentence.

findings_all.quote: This can be useful for tests of differences in treatment efficacy across treatment arms

Conversely, a too-short window is visible as a pre-trend only when pre-treatment horizons are requested; on a default run without horizons it contaminates the pooled reference silently. guide:419 and guide:463 repeat the claim.

Too large a value attenuates the pooled estimates, and the first # post-treatment horizons then read near zero. Request an event study to see either, and prefer the smallest defensible value.' findings_all.quote: A cluster() strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells, bootstrap() or permute() gives valid cell inference.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: When a treated cohort-by-period cell lies wholly inside one cluster, a cluster bootstrap cannot recover that cell's own sampling variance. A cell that sits in one cluster is resampled whole or not at all, so its idiosyncratic noise never varies across replications. Only the control-side noise does. The bootstrap cell standard error is therefore understated for exactly the cells the caution counts, just as the analytic one is. Probe p1 used 30 units with a unit-level i, cluster(unit), 10 treated units, iid N(0,1) errors and no effect. The theoretical sd of a cell estimate is 1.12. The bootstrap(standard) reps(200) cell standard errors were .19 to .32, and several null cells printed p = 0. The analytic cell standard errors were .22 to .34. The att row is fine under the bootstrap: .249 against a Monte Carlo sd of .257, because the resampling does vary across treated units. The caution also prints inside the bootstrap run itself (log line 65), where it claims that the run just made gives valid cell inference. The permute() half is false by the help's own account: help L441-442 and L909 say the gteffects cells carry no inference under permute(). The same claim appears in help L316 (the remedies list covers the gteffects cells), help L909 ('under bootstrap() the cell inference is bootstrap-based', which implies it is valid), guide L200 (rule 2: 'gteffects cells are understated (cautioned). Use bootstrap() ... or permute()') and guide L214.
findings_all.correct_statement: Whether the variance is analytic or from resampling, a parameter identified from a single cluster's data has a variance that no cluster-level procedure can estimate. The cluster's own noise enters the estimate once and is never re-drawn. Only a cluster() strictly finer than the cell, so that several independent units lie inside each cell, gives valid cell inference. bootstrap() is valid for the aggregate rows, which average over many treated clusters. It is not valid for single contained cells. permute() posts no cell inference at all.
findings_all.reference: Conley and Taber (2011), 'Inference with Difference in Differences with a Small Number of Policy Changes', Review of Economics and Statistics 93(1):113-125; MacKinnon and Webb (2018), 'The wild bootstrap for few (treated) clusters', Econometrics Journal 21(2):114-135, sec. 2, which shows that the scores of a single treated cluster are identically zero and that neither the CRVE nor a cluster bootstrap sees that cluster's variance.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Caution text (needs the author's wording clearance under the new-message rule): 'Caution: `gtcontain' of `gtn' e(gteffects) cell(s) lie wholly inside a single `gtcmode', so their se, p and interval columns are understated and the cell interval does not cover at its nominal level. This holds under bootstrap() too, since a cell inside one cluster is resampled whole. Only a cluster() strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells gives valid cell inference. The aggregate rows are a separate question, discussed under Standard Errors in the help.' Help L316: append '{it:bootstrap()} and {it:permute()} do not repair the {it:gteffects} cells: a cell inside one cluster is resampled whole, so its bootstrap standard error is understated as well, and {it:permute()} leaves the cells blank.' Help L909: replace 'under {it:bootstrap()} the cell inference is bootstrap-based' with 'under {it:bootstrap()} the cell inference is bootstrap-based, and it is understated for the cells the caution counts'. Guide L200: change the end of rule 2 to 'Use `bootstrap()` or `permute()` for the aggregate rows and tests. No engine repairs the `gteffects` cells in this design; only a finer `cluster()` does.' Do NOT build the blue-sky R1 requirement to gate this caution off under bootstrap(). The caution is true there.
findings_all.code_site: wooldid.ado 4949 (caution text); 2341-2377 (containment count, runs on the observed fit of bootstrap runs too); gteffects rewiring in wooldid_bootcellsx 7600ff
findings_all.ruling_checked: grep 'valid cell inference', 'gt_ncontained', 'GTE-4', 'containment' over review_process/. The only hit is review_process/blue_sky_2026-09-18/fix_proposal_status.md:407 and :412, where reviewer R1 asserted that 'the caution is false on every bootstrap() and permute() run' and 'Required: gate the caution display' off under the engines. That rests on the premise my probe refutes, and the requirement was not built (the caution fires under bootstrap at 925d0e8). No author ruling on whether bootstrap repairs the cells.

findings_all.quote: 3. **`robust`** is appropriate when errors are independent across observations, which is rare in a panel; it does not carry the cell-containment problem, and the analytic `ame` standard errors are identified under it.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: With a unit-level i on a unit-by-period panel, each treated cell is one observation with leverage 1. Its own dummy drives its residual to exactly zero, so the heteroskedasticity-robust meat omits that observation's noise and the att standard error is understated. This is the same blind spot as cell containment. The code already treats it that way: ado 2366-2375 counts one-row cells under robust as contained, and the gteffects caution fires. Help L907 and L992 say so as well. The guide's decision rule contradicts both. Probe p2 on the p1 design gave a robust att se of .212 against a Monte Carlo sd of .257, 0.82 of the truth. The pre-pare-down help (62b121c) measured 0.64 and 70% coverage for a cell. Guide L105 repeats the error where it matters most, in the paragraph on when a fine i is right: 'Even then, prefer `robust` or a `cluster()` finer than the cell for the analytic run'. With one row per unit-period no cluster finer than the cell exists, and robust has the same defect.
findings_all.correct_statement: Under robust a treated cell holding a single observation contributes a zero residual, so its variance is missing from the sandwich and the standard errors are understated. robust avoids this only when every treated cell holds several observations.
findings_all.reference: Chesher and Jewitt (1987), 'The Bias of a Heteroskedasticity Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimator', Econometrica 55(5):1217-1222 (HC estimators have zero weight at leverage-one points); MacKinnon and White (1985), Journal of Econometrics 29(3):305-325.
findings_all.proposed_fix: L201: '3. **`robust`** is appropriate when errors are independent across observations, which is rare in a panel. It avoids the cell-containment problem only when every treated cell holds several observations. With a unit-level `i` each treated cell is one observation whose residual is zero, and the standard errors are understated as they are under `cluster()` at `i`. The analytic `ame` standard errors are identified under it.' L105: replace the last sentence with 'Even then the analytic standard errors are understated, because every treated cell is a single observation under any `cluster()` and under `robust`. Use `bootstrap()` or `permute()` for inference on the aggregate rows.'
findings_all.code_site: wooldid.ado 2366-2375 (robust branch of the gteffects containment count)
findings_all.ruling_checked: grep 'robust' with 'containment' in review_process/changes_review_2026-09-22.md and blue_sky fix_proposal_status.md. GTE proposals measured the robust arm at 0.64 and 70% (proposals_GTE.md 'A1 arm 2 (robust, no cluster()) undercovers at 70%'). No ruling says robust escapes containment.

findings_all.quote: put the unit identifier in `fe()`, and cluster at the unit level or at any level strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The docs give 'finer than the cohort-by-period cells' as a sufficient condition for the cluster level. They never state the standard necessary condition: clusters must be no finer than the level at which treatment is assigned, and at least as coarse as the error dependence. Read literally, 'any level strictly finer' includes observation-level clustering, which is robust. Take a state policy studied on county or individual data, with i the onset cohort and cluster(county) chosen by rule 1 (L199: 'Cluster below the level of `i`'). Both texts endorse that pairing, and it is anti-conservative. Help L316 ('a {it:cluster()} strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells') has the same gap.
findings_all.correct_statement: Cluster at the level at which treatment is assigned, or coarser, and at least at the level of the error dependence. Within that constraint, prefer a level whose groups lie inside the cohort-by-period cells. When assignment is at the level of i itself, no valid analytic level exists that is finer than the cells. There, use bootstrap() for the aggregates or permute().
findings_all.reference: Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2023), 'When Should You Adjust Standard Errors for Clustering?', Quarterly Journal of Economics 138(1):1-35; Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan (2004), 'How Much Should We Trust Differences-in-Differences Estimates?', QJE 119(1):249-275.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Guide L95: '... put the unit identifier in `fe()`, and cluster at the level at which treatment is assigned, usually the unit, provided that level is finer than the cohort-by-period cells.' Guide L199: add 'Never cluster below the level at which treatment is assigned: a state policy needs `cluster(state)` even on county data. If the assignment level is `i` itself, use `bootstrap()` or `permute()` instead.' Help L316: 'The remedies are a {it:cluster()} at the treatment-assignment level that is strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells, {it:bootstrap()}, or {it:permute()}.'
findings_all.ruling_checked: grep 'assignment level', 'level of assignment', 'Abadie', 'cluster below' over review_process/. Found only SI-A1 (open_defects.md:301, author ruling 2026-09-10): 'clustering below the level of i is the intended practice'. That ruling is about i, not about the assignment level, and this finding adds a constraint without overturning it. The ado comment at 7436 ('cluster() is a claim about dependence and assignment') shows the author holds this view. It just is not in the docs.

findings_all.quote: Intuitively, this ought to be true whenever samples are large enough that sampling variation in covariates is ignorable (more precisely, ignorable within cohort-time period cells).
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The gap between conditional and unconditional standard errors does not shrink with sample size. Both variances are O(1/N). The extra unconditional term is the variance, across the treated sample, of the unit-level effect implied by the covariates and cell membership, scaled by 1/N. It is large whenever treatment effects are heterogeneous across cells or covariate values, and zero only when they are homogeneous. Probe p2 used two treated cohorts with effects 0 and 4 and unit clusters. The unconditional-to-conditional se ratio was 2.23 at 60 units and 2.29 at 600 units. The same misconception is in guide L307, which copies the paragraph, and in guide L202 (rule 4: 'when sampling variation in covariates or in the dose matters (small samples, influential weights)').
findings_all.correct_statement: Conditional (delta-method) standard errors are for the effect averaged over the treated units actually in the sample. Unconditional standard errors are for the population average. The two differ by a term that reflects heterogeneity of the effect across cells and covariate values. That term does not vanish as the sample grows, so the choice depends on the estimand and on effect heterogeneity, not on sample size.
findings_all.reference: Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2020), 'Sampling-Based versus Design-Based Uncertainty in Regression Analysis', Econometrica 88(1):265-296; Imbens (2004), 'Nonparametric Estimation of Average Treatment Effects under Exogeneity: A Review', Review of Economics and Statistics 86(1):4-29, sec. on population versus sample average effects.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Help L325-327: 'Does using unconditional standard errors make a large difference? Wooldridge (2025) expresses the view that conditional and unconditional standard errors often should be similar. They are similar when treatment effects vary little across cohort-period cells and covariate values. Where effects are heterogeneous the unconditional standard errors are larger, and the gap does not shrink as the sample grows: the conditional standard errors describe the effect averaged over the sampled treated units, the unconditional ones the population average. Sample weights that make particular observations very influential widen the gap further.' Keep the rest of the paragraph. Mirror the change in guide L307. Guide L202: '4. **`unconditionalse`** when the target is the population average effect and effects vary across cells or covariate values (not merely when samples are small).'
findings_all.ruling_checked: grep 'ignorable', 'conditional and unconditional', 'unconditional standard errors often' over review_process/: no ruling. The paragraph dates from the 2023/2024 help voice.

findings_all.quote: The default estimates standard errors in the underlying regression and then obtains standard errors on the treatment effects produced by the margins calculation using the delta method.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: Nowhere do the help or the guide say what the variance estimator is when neither cluster() nor robust is given. The code passes no vce to reghdfe (ado 1923-1925), so the default is the conventional homoskedastic, serially independent OLS variance. ppmlhdfe defaults to robust, and pweights force robust. In a difference-in-differences panel with serially correlated errors that default is badly anti-conservative. Nine of the fifteen help examples (1-10 except 0) show unclustered runs with no remark. The gteffects screen also skips the iid case (ado 2340).
findings_all.correct_statement: Without cluster(), robust, customvce() or pweights, the linear path reports conventional OLS standard errors, which assume independent homoskedastic errors. In panel difference-in-differences these typically overstate precision, and cluster() at the treatment-assignment level is the usual choice.
findings_all.reference: Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan (2004), QJE 119(1):249-275; Cameron and Miller (2015), 'A Practitioner's Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference', Journal of Human Resources 50(2):317-372, sec. II.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Help, after L145: 'Without {it:cluster()}, {it:robust}, {it:customvce()} or pweights, the linear regression reports conventional standard errors that assume independent, homoskedastic errors ({it:ppmlhdfe} is robust by default). On panel data these usually overstate precision; specify {it:cluster()} at the level at which treatment is assigned.' Guide ch. 4, new rule 0: '**Specify a variance.** With no `cluster()` or `robust` the linear path uses conventional OLS standard errors, which ignore serial correlation within units and are rarely appropriate in a panel.'

findings_all.quote: Each reported row uses a t distribution with degrees of freedom one less than the number of clusters contributing to that row
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The Ibragimov-Muller t test is guaranteed valid (conservative) under heterogeneous cluster variances only for two-sided levels alpha <= 0.083 or so. The docs say level() governs every interval, and level() accepts 10 to 99.99. At level(90), common in economics, IM intervals and p-values are outside the range the method's validity result covers, and the docs say nothing.
findings_all.correct_statement: IM inference is valid for tests at significance levels up to about 8.3 percent, which means confidence levels of about 91.7 percent or more. Below that the t(q-1) reference can over-reject when cluster estimates have unequal variances.
findings_all.reference: Ibragimov and Muller (2010), JBES 28(4):453-468, Theorem 1; Bakirov and Szekely (2006), 'Student's t-test for Gaussian scale mixtures', Journal of Mathematical Sciences 139(3):6497-6505.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Append to help L277: 'The Ibragimov and Muller result holds for tests at levels up to about 8.3 percent, so under {it:impvalues} a {it:level()} below about 92 is outside it.' Add the same sentence to the guide's impvalues entry (L226).

findings_all.quote: so a cluster's total mass stays proportional to its size in every replication - exactly as under the pairs cluster bootstrap, whose first two moments it shares -
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The claim is loose. Scaled Dirichlet(1,...,1) weights G*p_g have mean 1, variance (G-1)/(G+1) and covariance -1/(G+1). Multinomial pairs-bootstrap counts have mean 1, variance (G-1)/G and covariance -1/G. The means agree exactly, but the second moments differ by the factor G/(G+1), so the Bayesian bootstrap variance of a linear statistic is G/(G+1) times the pairs-bootstrap variance. With 10 clusters that is 9 percent of variance. The same phrase is in the few-treated-cluster caution (ado 10111: 'the Bayesian bootstrap, which shares the pairs cluster bootstrap's first two moments'). The blue-sky boot-bayes agent also measured a 36 percent sd gap under one dominant weight.
findings_all.correct_statement: The Bayesian bootstrap weights share the pairs bootstrap's first moment. Their second moments agree only up to a factor G/(G+1), so the Bayesian bootstrap variance is slightly smaller with few clusters.
findings_all.reference: Rubin (1981), 'The Bayesian Bootstrap', Annals of Statistics 9(1):130-134 (the n/(n+1) variance factor).
findings_all.proposed_fix: Guide L283: 'exactly as under the pairs cluster bootstrap, whose weight moments it matches to within a factor G/(G+1) in the variance'. Caution at ado 10111 (author clearance needed): 'the Bayesian bootstrap, whose weights match the pairs cluster bootstrap's in mean and nearly in variance'.

findings_all.quote:
Neither mode is a remedy for few treated clusters and no wild cluster bootstrap is offered; use {it:permute()} there, or
{help boottest} on the underlying regression outside {it:wooldid}.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The sentence offers the wild cluster bootstrap (boottest) as a remedy for few treated clusters, the condition the caution fires on (fewer than 6 treated). With very few treated clusters the restricted wild cluster bootstrap is known to under-reject severely, often with near-zero power, and the unrestricted version over-rejects. It is not a reliable fix in that range. The same advice is in the runtime caution at ado 10111 ('or the wild cluster bootstrap-t (boottest, on the stage-1 regression outside wooldid)').
findings_all.correct_statement: With one to a few treated clusters no cluster bootstrap, wild or pairs, is reliably sized. The restricted wild cluster bootstrap becomes very conservative, and its subcluster variants help only partly.
findings_all.reference: MacKinnon and Webb (2017), 'Wild Bootstrap Inference for Wildly Different Cluster Sizes', Journal of Applied Econometrics 32(2):233-254; MacKinnon and Webb (2018), Econometrics Journal 21(2):114-135.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Help L364-365: 'Neither mode is a remedy for few treated clusters, and neither is the wild cluster bootstrap, which becomes very conservative there; use {it:permute()}.' Make the matching change to the caution at ado 10111 (author clearance needed).

findings_all.quote: There the plain share stands, which is also what `bootstrap`'s own *estat bootstrap* reports;
findings_all.what_is_wrong: estat bootstrap reports bias, the bootstrap standard error and the normal, percentile, bc and bca confidence intervals. It reports no p-values, so it cannot report the plain share as a p-value. The code's convention (2 min(m0, m1)/n, the exact inversion of the percentile interval) is sound. Only the attribution is wrong.
findings_all.correct_statement: The plain share is the p-value dual to the percentile interval that estat bootstrap reports. estat bootstrap itself prints intervals, not p-values.
findings_all.reference: Stata [R] bootstrap postestimation, estat bootstrap.
findings_all.proposed_fix: 'There the plain share stands: it is the p-value dual to the percentile interval that `bootstrap`'s own *estat bootstrap* reports.'
findings_all.ruling_checked: The no-add-one convention for the percentile rows is ruled (ado 17706-17709 comment; guide L359). Only the estat bootstrap attribution is filed.

findings_all.quote: so that a treated cohort-by-period cell contains several clusters. That third one is not confined to clustering: `robust` with a unit-level *i* leaves each treated cell holding a single observation whose residual its own dummy drives to zero, and the same panel then gives 0.64 and 70%.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The guide's copy of the help paragraph has lost its core. The source (help at 62b121c) read: 'At or above the level of i the cluster-robust covariance stops seeing the treated cells' own variation, and three things follow: ... Measured on a 30-state panel ... 0.29 ... 44% ...'. Without it, 'That third one' and '0.64 and 70%' have no antecedent. The guide's Standard Errors section therefore never states the mechanism or the measured understatement it then offers remedies for. It has been this way since 08b0b7d.
findings_all.correct_statement: At or above the level of i the cluster-robust covariance cannot see the treated cells' own variation. The att rows' standard errors are understated, the joint pre-trend tests are oversized, and the gteffects cells fail hardest. robust with a unit-level i has the same cell-level failure.
findings_all.reference: Help text at commit 62b121c, Standard Errors, 'What level to cluster at'.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Replace the first two sentences after the heading with: 'The intended practice is to cluster **below** the level of *i*, at a level whose units are nested inside cohorts, so that a treated cohort-by-period cell contains several clusters. At or above the level of *i* the cluster-robust covariance cannot see the treated cells' own variation. The `att` rows' standard errors are then understated, the joint pre-trend tests are oversized, and the `gteffects` cells fail hardest. `robust` with a unit-level *i* fails the same way, because each treated cell is one observation whose residual its own dummy drives to zero.'
findings_all.ruling_checked: git log -S '0.64 and 70' shows the fragment entered the guide at 08b0b7d while the help (62b121c) still had the full paragraph. The help pare-down at 07dd933 removed it from the help. Not a ruling on content.

findings_all.quote: P-values are then obtained from a t-distribution with the residual degrees of freedom of the underlying regression.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The code threads the regression's e(df_r) into margins (ado 1995, 2552). Under cluster() reghdfe posts G-1 (the smallest G-1 under multi-way clustering), not the residual degrees of freedom. Under poisson, ppmlhdfe posts no df_r and the reference is the normal (the tables label z). The sentence describes neither case.
findings_all.correct_statement: P-values use a t distribution with the regression's e(df_r): G-1 under cluster(), the residual degrees of freedom otherwise, and the normal under poisson.
findings_all.reference: reghdfe help (df_r under vce(cluster)); Cameron and Miller (2015), JHR 50(2), sec. VI.
findings_all.proposed_fix: 'P-values are then obtained from a t-distribution with the degrees of freedom the regression reports: the number of clusters minus one under {it:cluster()}, and the residual degrees of freedom otherwise. Under {it:poisson} they are normal.'

findings_all.what_is_wrong: The recipe posts b and V without dof(), so a later test or lincom uses the normal and chi-squared. The printed event-study table uses t(e(df_r)), G-1 under cluster() and under the default bootdf(clusters). With few clusters the hand test is anti-conservative against the table: the 5% critical value is 1.96 against 2.26 at G = 10. The guide recipe at L829-831 is the same.

findings_all.quote: it protects only when the cluster-robust standard error is informative about the treated clusters - many observations per treated cohort-period cell, with `cluster()` coarser than the cell.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The text gives the wrong condition for permtstat to protect. The regression carries a dummy for each treated cohort-by-period cell, so the OLS residuals in each treated cell sum to exactly zero. When a single cluster contains the whole cell, that cluster's score on the cell dummy is this zero sum. So the cluster-robust variance cannot see the cell's own error variance, however many observations the cell holds. A cluster 'coarser than the cell' is exactly the failing case. The SE sees the treated cells' variance only when each treated cell spans several clusters, that is, with cluster() strictly finer than the cell. The repo says this itself in three places: guide ch.4 ('cluster below the level of i ... so that every treated cohort-by-period cell contains several clusters'), the jtcoarse caution (it calls the covariance degenerate when i is nested in the cluster), and the permonsetcohorts entry ('A finer cluster() is also what makes permtstat protective'). The consequence goes further than the text admits. Without permonsetcohorts, permute() requires cluster() to nest i, so every treated cell lies inside one cluster and permtstat can never protect. It can protect only under permonsetcohorts with several clusters per treated cohort-period cell. The same wrong condition appears in the runtime caution at ado:6948 (listed in ch.14 at guide:984). Help:465 and guide:372 name only 'cluster() equal to i', and the caution fires only when clus == ivar. A cluster strictly coarser than i, such as i = unit with cluster(state), which is the classic few-treated-states layout, fails in the same way but gets no caution. A reader following the text would believe a size remedy is in force when it structurally cannot be.
findings_all.correct_statement: The studentized statistic protects against a treated cluster with atypical error variance only when the cluster-robust SE sees that variance, which requires each treated cohort-by-period cell to contain several clusters (cluster() strictly finer than the cells). Under permute() this is possible only with permonsetcohorts. Whenever cluster() nests i (cluster() equal to i or coarser), every treated cell sits in one cluster and neither statistic is protected. A probe with i = cohort, cluster(state), fe(state) and permonsetcohorts shows permtstat behaving as the text intends in that configuration.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Guide 383: replace the quoted clause with: "it protects only when the cluster-robust standard error can see the treated clusters' own variance. That needs several clusters inside each treated cohort-period cell, with `cluster()` strictly finer than the cell. Under `permute()` only `permonsetcohorts` allows that. Whenever `cluster()` nests *i*, each treated cell sits inside one cluster and neither statistic is protected." Help 464-465: "It protects against a treated cluster with unusually dispersed errors only where several clusters lie inside each treated cohort-period cell, which under {it:permute()} needs {it:permonsetcohorts} with a {it:cluster()} finer than {it:i}; whenever {it:cluster()} nests {it:i} it does not, and a caution says so." Code: in the caution at ado:6948, change 'cluster() coarser than the cell' to 'several clusters inside each treated cohort-period cell'. Widen both cluster-at-i cautions (6948 and 6957) from clus == ivar to 'cluster() nests i and permonsetcohorts is not specified'. Both are changes to user-facing message wording and triggers, so the author must clear them first under the 2026-09-21 new-message rule.

findings_all.reference: OLS algebra of a saturated cell dummy (residuals sum to zero within the cell), with the cluster-robust sandwich score X_c'e_c; MacKinnon and Webb (2017, J. Applied Econometrics 32(2), 'Wild bootstrap inference for wildly different cluster sizes') on the CRVE's blindness to a treated cluster whose residuals are fitted away; MacKinnon and Webb (2020, J. Econometrics 218(2)) on RI-t.
findings_all.ruling_checked: Searched review_process/ for 'coarser than the cell', 'permtstat', 'cluster() at the i level' and 'MacKinnon'. rulings_2026-09-07.md asks for an exchangeability caution of permute()'s own and does not rule on the SE condition. research_2026-09-06/F058_permutation.md s6.8 measured permtstat at cluster(i) not normalising (null t SD 1.43-1.67), which is consistent with this finding. No ruling adopts 'coarser than the cell'.

findings_all.quote: Randomization inference assumes clusters are exchangeable in **assignment** and fails when onset is systematically related to the outcome path - which is the identifying assumption the design already needs.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The text says randomization inference needs nothing beyond the DiD identifying assumption. That is false. Random (exchangeable) assignment of onset is strictly stronger than parallel trends: random timing implies parallel trends, but parallel trends does not imply exchangeable assignment. In the model-based reading, where assignment is fixed and errors are random, the test also needs the treated clusters' errors to be distributed like the controls'. It fails when the treated clusters differ in size or variance even though parallel trends holds. The guide's own ch.6 (line 383) says exactly this. So does the author's ruling the paragraph was drawn from: rulings_2026-09-07.md says RI 'fails when treated clusters are heterogeneous in variance'. The guide paragraph therefore misstates the ruling, and it invites a reader to treat belief in parallel trends as sufficient for valid RI.
findings_all.correct_statement: Randomization inference is exact for the sharp null when onset was randomly (exchangeably) assigned across clusters. That assumption is stronger than parallel trends. When assignment is instead treated as fixed, validity needs the treated clusters to be exchangeable with the controls in their error distribution, and the test is mis-sized when they differ in size or variance even if parallel trends holds.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Replace the quoted sentence with: "Randomization inference assumes onset was assigned exchangeably across clusters. That is stronger than parallel trends, which the design already needs. It fails when the treated clusters differ systematically from the controls in size or error variance, even when parallel trends holds (MacKinnon and Webb 2020)."
findings_all.reference: Athey and Imbens (2022, J. Econometrics 226(1), 'Design-based analysis in difference-in-differences settings with staggered adoption'); Roth and Sant'Anna (2023, JPE Microeconomics, 'Efficient estimation for staggered rollout designs'), where random timing implies parallel trends but not conversely; MacKinnon and Webb (2020, J. Econometrics 218(2)).
findings_all.ruling_checked: grep 'orthogonal' and 'exchangeab' in review_process/: rulings_2026-09-07.md:208 (the source of the paragraph) says RI 'fails when treated clusters are heterogeneous in variance', and research_2026-09-08/engine_parity.md:46 is the same. The ruled claim that the two assumptions are orthogonal and different stands. Only the clause equating RI's assumption with the identifying assumption departs from the ruling.

findings_all.quote: A caution prints when fewer than 6 clusters are ever treated, since the set of distinct assignments is then small whatever {it:permreps()} is.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The counting claim is false in general. With k treated clusters at one onset among G clusters, the number of distinct assignments is C(G,k). For k = 5 that is 142,506 at G = 30 and 658,008 at G = 40. Sampled draws then almost never repeat, and the attainable p-values are not coarse. The advice the caution gives is also unavailable in exactly those cases, because permexact is refused above 65,534 assignments. The same claim is in guide:383 ('few ever-treated clusters means few distinct onset assignments, so sampled draws repeat ...') and in the runtime caution at ado:6972 (ch.14 guide:987). The caution fires on k < 6 without looking at the assignment count. The count M is computed later, in permrun, and the case of genuinely few assignments is already covered correctly by the 10-percent-of-M caution and the reported e(perm_npossible). With few treated clusters, the real concern is not resolution. It is that validity rests entirely on assignment exchangeability, and a handful of atypical treated clusters mis-sizes the test (MacKinnon and Webb 2020). So a user can be told their reference set is coarse when it has hundreds of thousands of elements, while the substantive few-treated risk goes unstated.
findings_all.correct_statement: The number of distinct assignments is the product over strata of the multinomial coefficients, C(G,k) for one onset. It is small only when G is small or k is 1 or 2, and it is reported in e(perm_npossible). With few treated clusters, the reason for caution is that the test's size depends entirely on the treated clusters being exchangeable with the controls.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Help 444: "A caution prints when fewer than 6 clusters are ever treated: with so few treated clusters the test's size rests entirely on their being exchangeable with the controls. The number of possible assignments is in {it:e(perm_npossible)}, and a separate caution prints when {it:permreps()} exceeds 10 percent of it." Guide 383: the same, in Markdown. Code: reword the caution at ado:6972 to that content (or move it into permrun and key it on wdp_npd). This changes a user-facing message, so the author must clear it first.
