findings_all.reference: Elementary combinatorics of the shuffle design (the count computed in wooldid_permx at ado:15550-15560); MacKinnon and Webb (2020, J. Econometrics 218(2)) for the few-treated-cluster risk.
findings_all.ruling_checked: Searched review_process/ for 'fewer than 6', 'distinct assignments', 'wdpntc' and 'ever treated'. rulings_2026-09-07.md (section I, 'the accidents') asked for permute()'s own EXCHANGEABILITY caution, and the built text makes a counting claim instead. The blue_sky MCBP-GUARD item concerns the bootstrap's treated-count guard, not this claim. No ruling endorses the claim that few treated clusters means few assignments.

findings_all.quote: Romano and Wolf max-|studentized| step-down computed from the same replications, which controls the family-wise error rate across the horizons.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The code (wooldid_permstep, ado:18307) implements the step-down correctly, and it is exact under the global sharp null that no horizon of the family has any effect. That gives weak FWER control. An unqualified 'controls the family-wise error rate' reads as strong control: control over the true nulls whatever the other horizons are doing. Strong control is precisely what makes a step-down worth more than the single-step max-t. It requires subset pivotality: the null distribution of the true-null horizons must not depend on the false ones. Here it does. A reassigned onset carries the effect at one horizon into the null draws of the other horizons, which is the same mechanism the text itself describes for the pre-treatment rows. So under partial alternatives, control is not established. Guide:403 has the same problem: 'It is exact under the sharp null of no effect at any horizon of the family and controls the family-wise error rate across those horizons'.
findings_all.correct_statement: The permutation step-down is exact, and controls the FWER, under the global sharp null of no effect at any horizon of the family (weak control). When some horizons have effects, reassigned onsets move those effects into the other horizons' null draws, so subset pivotality fails and strong control is not guaranteed.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Help 483-484: "... computed from the same replications. It controls the family-wise error rate across the horizons when no horizon of the family has any effect. When some horizons do, the reassigned onsets carry their effects into the other horizons' null draws, so control over the remaining horizons is not guaranteed." Guide 403: replace 'It is exact under the sharp null of no effect at any horizon of the family and controls the family-wise error rate across those horizons' with 'It is exact under the sharp null of no effect at any horizon of the family, and under that null it controls the family-wise error rate across those horizons. When some horizons have effects, reassigned onsets carry them into the other horizons' null draws, so control over the rest is not guaranteed.'
findings_all.reference: Westfall and Young (1993, Resampling-Based Multiple Testing, Wiley), subset pivotality as the condition for strong control; Romano and Wolf (2005, Econometrica 73(4), 'Exact and approximate stepdown methods for multiple hypothesis testing'), strong control under their monotonicity and null-distribution conditions.
findings_all.ruling_checked: Searched review_process/ for 'strong control', 'weak control', 'family-wise' and 'step-down'. research_2026-09-08/engine_parity.md itself says 'A permutation step-down is exact under the global sharp null'. rulings_2026-09-07.md rules only that the step-down stays permutation-only. No ruling asserts strong control.

findings_all.quote: It is not robust to the treated clusters being atypical in size or in error variance - relabelling then mixes clusters of different variance, and the reference distribution is narrower than the sampling distribution of the observed statistic (MacKinnon and Webb 2020).
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The text states only one direction. MacKinnon and Webb (2020) find both: RI over-rejects when the treated clusters are small or noisy relative to the controls, because the reference distribution is then narrower than the sampling distribution, and it under-rejects when they are large, because the reference distribution is then wider. A reader whose treated clusters are large would conclude that the permutation p-values are too small, when they are too large.
findings_all.correct_statement: When the treated clusters differ from the controls in size or error variance, the reference distribution and the sampling distribution of the observed statistic differ in spread. The test over-rejects when the treated clusters are smaller or noisier than the controls and under-rejects when they are larger or quieter.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Replace the quoted clause with: "It is not robust to the treated clusters being atypical in size or in error variance. Relabelling then mixes clusters of different variance, so the reference distribution is narrower than the observed statistic's sampling distribution when the treated clusters are small or noisy, and the test over-rejects, and wider when they are large, and it under-rejects (MacKinnon and Webb 2020)."
findings_all.reference: MacKinnon and Webb (2020, J. Econometrics 218(2), 'Randomization inference for difference-in-differences with few treated clusters'), simulations varying the treated clusters' share of observations.
findings_all.ruling_checked: grep 'narrower than the sampling' and 'MacKinnon' in review_process/: no ruling on the direction. rulings_2026-09-07.md says only 'fails when treated clusters are heterogeneous in variance', which does not specify a direction.

findings_all.quote: These contrasts and the across-subgroup equality tests answer the sharp null of no effect at any horizon, not equality of the subgroups' effects: a common nonzero effect alone can reject them
findings_all.what_is_wrong: Labelling these tests as sharp-null tests is correct. The directional claim that follows is not. A common effect tau leaves the observed contrast centred at zero, while reassigned onsets carry tau into the permuted contrasts and widen their reference distribution. So the observed contrast lands in the middle of a wider null, and the test loses power rather than rejecting. Probe (probes/econ_permute/probe.do: 40 states, cluster = i = state, subgroups by state, permstrata(sg), permreps(99)): with a common tau = 5, the contrast p-values were .80, .70 and .46 on three datasets. The SD of the contrast's null draws was .81 to .90, against .24 at tau = 0. The same sentence is printed in the run footer (ado:13221). The practical harm is that a reader may discount a genuine rejection as possibly driven by a common effect.
findings_all.correct_statement: The tests are of the sharp null, so they are not size-controlled for the null of equal but nonzero effects. A common nonzero effect widens their reference distribution, so they lose power against real differences between subgroups, and their p-values need not match the analytic equality test's.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Guide 383: replace 'a common nonzero effect alone can reject them' with 'a common nonzero effect widens their reference distribution, so they lose power against real differences between subgroups'. Footer at ado:13221: the same clause substitution. That is a change to author-approved wording, so it goes to him for clearance.
findings_all.code_site: wooldidinstall/wooldid.ado:13221 (footer sentence)
findings_all.reference: Randomization-test logic for a non-sharp null: under a constant effect the permutation distribution of the contrast is centred near zero and inflated by the relocated effect (Rosenbaum 2002, Observational Studies, ch. 2, on tests of sharp nulls under constant effects). Probe results are in probes/econ_permute/probe.log.
findings_all.ruling_checked: changes_review_2026-09-22.md:68 ('Label as the sharp null now'; footer text approved, built 66d6680) contains this exact clause. The ruling's substance, labelling the tests as sharp-null tests, stands. The finding concerns only the directional sub-clause, which the probe contradicts.

findings_all.quote: With `contreat()` the dose stays with its unit and only onset timing is re-randomized (the null: timing as-if random given dose)
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The parenthesis calls the assignment assumption the null. What is tested is still the sharp null of no treatment effect on any outcome. Onset being as-if random given dose is the randomization assumption that makes the reference distribution valid for that null. The code comment at ado:6655 uses the same shorthand.
findings_all.correct_statement: The test is of the sharp null of no effect, and it is valid when onset timing was assigned as-if randomly given each unit's dose.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Replace the parenthesis with: "(the test is of the sharp null of no effect, valid when onset timing was assigned as if at random given dose)".
findings_all.reference: Fisher's sharp null and the randomization distribution (Imbens and Rubin 2015, Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences, ch. 5).
findings_all.ruling_checked: grep 'as-if random given dose' and 'timing as-if' in review_process/: no hits. The phrase appears only in the guide and in the ado comment at 6655.

findings_all.quote: if `amelive' == 0 & `amedrop' > 0 {
findings_all.what_is_wrong: When some treated cohort-period cells have no within-cell dose variation (their dose slope is dropped for collinearity) but others do, the dropped slopes enter margins dydx(contreat) as exact zeros that keep their full weight. The reported ame (and ame_it, ame_i, ame_itime, the ES_ame rows and the cfx ame cells) is then attenuated toward zero by the weight share of unidentified cells. The void screen fires only when every treated slope is dropped. Measured (probe p2): 3 equal treated cohorts, true dose slope 1 in every cell, one cohort's dose constant within cohort: ame = .6668 (se .0004), exactly 2/3 of the value computed from the two identified cohorts. The only message is the generic 'a treatment period coefficient interacted with something ... was dropped' caution, which does not say the ame is biased, and under lattice() with verbose off even that caution is suppressed.
findings_all.correct_statement: A treated cell whose dose slope is not identified has no ame. The estimand the help defines (a weighted average of within-cell dose slopes over treated observations) can only be formed over the cells whose slope is identified; averaging in a structural zero for the others is not an estimate of anything. This is the same logic the author already applied to the all-dropped case.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Two options for the author, both small. (a) Extend the existing amevoid predicate at wooldid.ado:13536 from `amelive == 0 & amedrop > 0` to `amedrop > 0` restricted to cells that have rows and a nonzero dose (the token loop already knows which cells are dropped), and void the ame family as the all-dropped case does. (b) Keep the estimate but renormalize it: build a tempvar flagging treated rows of cells with a live dose slope (keyed on _i,_t, and the lattice bin when present) and add `& flag` to the subpop() of every ame margins call (2899, 2915, 2954, 2970, 3114, 3203, 3248, 3312, 3359, 3364, 3871, 3890, 3918, 4097, 4110, 4141, 4191, 4199, 4256, 14013, 14051), reporting the excluded weight share. Either needs a caution worded with the author under the new-message rule. Help sentence to add under contreat(): {it:If only some treated cohort-period cells lack dose variation, their dose slopes are not identified, and the ame averages over the remaining cells only.} (option b) or {it:...and the ame results are reported as missing.} (option a).
findings_all.reference: Definition of the average marginal effect as a weighted mean of identified derivatives (Wooldridge 2010, Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, 2nd ed., sec. 2.2.5); an unidentified coefficient normalised to zero by a collinearity drop is not an estimate of that coefficient.

findings_all.quote: pieces without it are dropped for collinearity, the reported average marginal effect then averages only the pieces that survived, and the analytic standard errors can be far smaller than the estimates' sampling variability
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The ame does not average only the surviving pieces. Because the lattice enters as i.cell##i.lat##c.dose, a single-valued cell-by-bin piece loses its slope DEVIATION term and silently inherits the cell's base-bin slope. Measured (probe p3b): true bin slopes 1, 3, 5; cohort 1's bin-3 piece single-valued; the implied slope for that piece is 1.008 (truth 5), cfx ame bin 3 = 3.80 against 5, headline ame 2.48 against 2.90, and no caution prints (the dropped-term caution is gated off under lattice() without verbose). Probe p3 (piece in bin 2) gives the same base-bin inheritance. The same wrong sentence is at guide 593 ('averages only the pieces that survived') and guide pitfall 1383 ('the ame averages only the survivors'). The SE clause is also on the wrong mechanism: both adversarial rounds of the blue-sky LAT L4 review measured that the understated standard errors come from saturated pieces whose slope is still identified, not from single-valued pieces.
findings_all.correct_statement: A treated cell-by-bin piece with fewer than two distinct doses has no identified slope of its own. wooldid then drops that piece's slope deviation and the piece takes the slope of its cell's base bin, so the ame and the plotted bin ame average in a slope the data never estimated. Separately, a piece with no more observations than parameters is fitted exactly, and the analytic standard errors can then be far smaller than the sampling variability.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Help 791-795 replacement: {pstd} Take care also not to over-saturate the specification with lattice terms. Each treated cohort-period cell must hold at least two distinct values of Contreat_jt within each lattice bin it occupies. A piece without them has no slope of its own. {it:wooldid} then gives it the slope of the cell's lowest bin, and the reported average marginal effect and the plotted bin effects include that borrowed slope. No caution prints unless {it:verbose} is given. A piece with no more observations than parameters is fitted exactly, and the analytic standard errors can then be far smaller than the estimates' sampling variability. A useful rule of thumb is that the number of units contributing to a treated cell should be several times the number of lattice bins. {p_end}. Guide 593: replace 'the pieces with fewer than two distinct values are dropped for collinearity, the reported average marginal effect then averages only the pieces that survived' with 'a piece with fewer than two distinct values has no slope of its own and takes the slope of its cell's lowest bin, which the average marginal effect then includes; a piece with no more observations than parameters is fitted exactly'. Guide 1383: '15. A lattice with more bins than units per cell: a piece without dose variation takes its cell's lowest-bin slope, so the `ame` includes slopes the data never estimated.'
findings_all.reference: Factor-variable ## parameterisation: with main-slope plus deviation coding, dropping a deviation restricts that level's slope to the base level's (StataCorp, [U] 11.4.3 Factor variables; [R] regress collinearity handling).

findings_all.quote: When specified, {it:wooldid} will still present ATT-type average treatment effects estimates, which in this case should essentially be the integral of the estimated average marginal effects across the distribution of the continuous treatment variable.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: Under contreatwithin the att is a mixture, and the event study steps down mechanically at the last onset. In periods that still hold a not-yet-treated unit, the cohort-period intercept is identified and the att carries the full level effect of treatment. In periods where every unit is treated, the intercepts are collinear with the time effects. contreatwithin rewrites the working safety to off, so the dropped-dummy screen is skipped, one intercept per period is normalised to zero without a message, and only there does the att reduce to the dose-slope integral (relative to an arbitrarily chosen cohort). Measured (probe p4): onsets at t=3 and t=5, no never-treated units, true effect 1 + d (mean d 2.03, so true att 3.03 and slope integral 2.03). Reported att 2.366. ES post0 2.545 = one half of (3.03 + 2.03), because the onset-3 cohorts still have a not-yet-treated comparison at t=3 but the onset-5 cohorts have none at t=5. post2 = 2.023, the pure slope integral. The result is a spurious decline across horizons, and no caution prints. Relabelling the cohorts moves the att (2.366 to 2.368), which shows the normalisation depends on the solver. Even where every intercept is removed (for example i-by-t effects in fe()), the att is a linear extrapolation of the dose response down to dose zero, and it assumes that dose zero means untreated. The same sentence is at guide 603.
findings_all.correct_statement: Without an untreated comparison, the level effect of treatment in a cohort-period cell is identified only while some unit is still untreated in that period. Where no unit is, the cell intercepts are not identified and wooldid sets them to zero. The att there is only the dose part, the effect of moving from dose zero to the observed dose, extrapolated along the fitted slope. The reported att and its event study therefore mix the two kinds of period, and they can change sharply at the last onset for that reason alone. The ame does not depend on this and is the quantity to read.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Help 817-818 (and guide 603 in Markdown), replace the sentence with: When specified, {it:wooldid} still reports att estimates, but read them with care. The level effect of treatment in a cohort-period cell is identified only while some unit is untreated in that period. Where every unit is treated, the cell intercepts are not identified, and {it:wooldid} sets them to zero without a message. The att there is only the effect of moving from a dose of zero to the observed dose, extrapolated along the estimated slope. The reported att and its event study mix these two kinds of period, and can drop at the last onset for that reason alone. Rely on the ame results under {it:contreatwithin}. Optionally (author's call, new-message rule applies): count the treated cell dummies dropped under contreatwithin in wooldid_ccscreen (whose dropped-dummy loop is skipped when sw is off, wooldid.ado:13372) and print one caution naming the affected periods.
findings_all.reference: Level effects in two-way designs are identified only against units untreated in the same period (Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess 2024, REStud, 'Revisiting Event-Study Designs', Proposition on identification with no never-treated units; Wooldridge 2025 on not-yet-treated comparisons).

That makes the relaxation a ruled design; what is not ruled is the help's statement of what the att then equals, which the probe shows is false in staggered designs.

findings_all.quote: these different g() options set the reference effect of Contreat_jt relative to which Contreat_jt effects are estimated in treated cells.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The help and guide present the ame as 'the average marginal effect of the continuous treatment' and describe byTime as 'analogous to the second diff', but they never state the condition under which a within-cell slope across units has a causal reading. The ame is the slope, across treated units in the same cell, of the treatment effect in the dose, net of a reference slope. Parallel trends in untreated outcomes across dose levels identifies ATT(d|d) at each dose. It does not make the difference across doses a causal response. That also needs no selection on gains: higher-dose units must not have larger effects at every dose (the strong parallel trends assumption). Without it the ame equals the average causal response plus a selection-bias term. The same applies to the slope of the cfx att plot across dose bins. 'A bit speculative' (help 175) is a hedge, not the condition. The help's line 173 ('estimates of the effect of the continuous treatment variable can be computed within each treated i-t cell') and guide chapter 9 carry the same unqualified reading.
findings_all.correct_statement: Under parallel trends in untreated outcomes across dose levels (given the chosen g()), the att at each dose is identified. The ame, and the differences in att across the cfx bins, measure the causal effect of more dose only under the stronger condition that units at different doses would have had the same treatment effects at any given dose. Otherwise they also carry selection bias from sorting into dose.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Help, new paragraph after line 804: {pstd} What the ame measures. Within a treated cell, the ame compares units that received different doses. It is the causal effect of a marginal increase in the dose only if units at different doses would have followed the same path without treatment, and would also have gained the same from treatment at any given dose. The second condition is the strong parallel trends assumption of Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024). Without it, the ame also carries selection bias, since higher-dose units may simply be units with larger effects. The same holds for differences in att across the bins of the continuous treatment effects plots. {p_end} Guide chapter 9, decision rule 1, add: 'The ame is causal only under strong parallel trends (Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna 2024): units at different doses must share both untreated trends and treatment-effect functions.'
findings_all.reference: Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024), 'Difference-in-Differences with a Continuous Treatment', NBER WP 32117 / arXiv 2107.02637, Theorems 3.1-3.3: standard parallel trends identifies ATT(d|d); comparisons across doses (ACRT) require strong parallel trends, else ACRT plus selection bias.
findings_all.ruling_checked: grep -rni 'goodman-bacon|strong parallel|callaway|selection bias|ACRT|selection on gains' over review_process/ found only an unrelated blue-sky note on missing package comparisons (structure_and_ux.md:870). There is no ruling on the identifying assumption for the ame.

findings_all.quote: the joint pre-trend and adversarial tests are not calibrated, the `ame` standard errors under `contreat()` are not identified, and the `gteffects` cells' intervals do not cover.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The bullet is about a unit-level i, where every treated cell holds one observation. There the ame POINT ESTIMATE is not identified. Every cell's dose slope is dropped, and the amevoid screen reports the whole ame family as missing (help contreat() entry). The cell-containment caution the sentence alludes to does not fire, because single-row cells are exempt (help 825, wooldid_amescreen detect: amerows >= 2). Saying only that the ame standard errors are not identified suggests the ame itself is usable in that design, and that finer clustering or the bootstrap would rescue it. They would not.
findings_all.correct_statement: With a unit-level i, no treated cell has within-cell dose variation, so the ame itself is not identified; wooldid reports the ame results as missing, and no clustering or resampling choice changes that.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Guide 92: replace 'the `ame` standard errors under `contreat()` are not identified' with 'under `contreat()` the `ame` itself is not identified, since a one-row cell has no dose variation, and wooldid reports it as missing'.
findings_all.reference: A within-cell slope requires at least two distinct regressor values in the cell (rank condition).

findings_all.quote: draws the ame continuous treatment effects plots without confidence intervals; the att results are unaffected.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The same design, with every treated cell inside one cluster, also understates the att standard errors: each cell's residuals sum to zero within its cluster, so the cell's own sampling variance never enters the sandwich. The help says so at 316 ('the att rows' analytic standard errors are understated without a caution'), guide 649 says so, and the code's own caution says '(and with some adverse implications for the ATTs as well)'. A reader of this paragraph alone would take the att inference as sound.
findings_all.correct_statement: The screen leaves the att rows as they are, but in this design their analytic standard errors are understated too.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Replace 'the att results are unaffected.' with 'the att rows are still reported, but their analytic standard errors are understated in this design as well (see {help wooldid##standarderrors:Discussion of What Level to Cluster At}).'
findings_all.reference: Cluster-robust variance with regressors constant within cluster-contained cells: the score for cell-specific parameters sums to zero within each cluster (Cameron and Miller 2015, JHR, 'A Practitioner's Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference', sec. IV on fixed effects nested in clusters).

findings_all.quote: or a {it:cluster()} strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: This states the validity condition in partition language, and read literally it is wrong. A cluster 'strictly finer than the cells' would be nested inside cells, for example unit-by-period, which is close to robust. The standard remedy with a coarse i, clustering on the unit, is not finer than the cells: a unit spans several cells. What matters, and what the screen tests (nunique clusters per cell == 1), is that no treated cell lies inside a single cluster. The same phrase is at help 316, 561 and 662 and guide 511 and 649.
findings_all.correct_statement: Valid analytic ame inference needs a cluster() under which every treated cohort-by-period cell spans several clusters, as clustering on the unit does when i is a cohort.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Help 826 (and the twins): replace 'a {it:cluster()} strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells' with 'a {it:cluster()} that splits every treated cohort-by-period cell across several clusters, such as the unit when {it:i} is a cohort'.
findings_all.reference: Cameron and Miller (2015), JHR, sec. IV: cluster-robust inference requires within-cluster score variation for each parameter.

findings_all.quote: If this option is specified when the always 0 condition is not met, {it:wooldid} will return poorly identified estimates.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The problem is bias, not weak identification. untreatedZero sets g() = 0, so a nonzero dose in untreated observations leaves its baseline effect in the error term. The treated-cell slopes then absorb that baseline slope. The att is also shifted by the baseline effect times the change in the mean dose between the reference and treated periods. The estimates can be precise and wrong, and 'poorly identified' suggests noise. Guide 583 and pitfall 1382 repeat it.
findings_all.correct_statement: If the dose is not zero outside treated cohort-periods, untreatedZero omits its baseline effect, and the ame and att are biased by it, however precise they look.
findings_all.proposed_fix: Replace 'will return poorly identified estimates' with 'omits the baseline effect of the dose, and the ame and att estimates are then biased, however precise they appear'. Guide pitfall 1382: '14. `contreatcontrols(untreatedZero)` when the dose is not zero outside treated cells: the baseline dose effect is omitted and the estimates are biased, with no error.'
findings_all.reference: Omitted variable bias (Wooldridge 2010, Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, sec. 4.3).
findings_all.ruling_checked: No ruling on this wording; the untreatedZero rulings (R5, uz-cellconstant-dose) concern the constant-dose refusal.

findings_all.quote: {it:ES_att_post#} (the event-study horizons, numbered outward from the reference period)
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The code names each horizon by its relative period, not by its distance from the reference period. The names are built as post`relyr' / pre`abs(relyr)' (wooldid.ado 2771-2772, 4326-4365, 4645-4647). The probe confirms it: esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(4) returns pre5, pre4, pre3 and pre2 with relyr -5 to -2, and there is no pre1 because -1 is the reference. Under the pooled default the reference is a pool of the earliest periods. There, pre1 (relative period -1) is the horizon FARTHEST from the reference, so reading the sentence literally reverses the order of the pre-period horizons. Under esrelativeto(-3) the two readings differ by two periods. The same wrong sentence is at guide line 15 ('pre# and post# counted outward from the reference period') and guide line 841 (a copy of the help sentence). A user who writes lincom or test on ES_att_pre#, or who reads the timing of a pre-trend off the names, gets the wrong horizon.
findings_all.correct_statement: pre# is relative period -# and post# is relative period #. post0 is the effective onset period. The reference period is never a column. Under esfixedbaseperiod at the default esrelativeto(-1), the pre columns therefore start at pre2.

findings_all.lens: event study, pre-trends, adversarial test and bands

findings_all.quote: the line is chosen to fit the estimates as well as possible, a null that is adversarial toward finding pre-trend violations.
findings_all.what_is_wrong: The null is stated correctly, and the author ruled it (BS-12, one-parameter line through the reference). The interpretation is what fails. The option is called the 'adversarial pre-trend test' in every message, and the help frames it as a pre-trend diagnostic. But its null covers the POST-treatment coefficients too: the whole event-study path, pre and post, lies on one line through the reference. So any genuine treatment effect that does not happen to continue a line rejects it. The probe shows this: on dta_binary, with flat pre-trends (joint pre-trend p = .75 and .81) and a real effect, the adversarial p is 5e-14. A reader who takes a small 'adversarial pre-trend' p as a detected pre-trend violation draws the wrong inference. Nothing in the help or the guide says that rejection is expected whenever there is a real effect, or how to read the test beside jointtests. The guide copy at line 451 has the same sentence.
findings_all.correct_statement: The null is what a linear differential trend with no treatment effect would produce: every coefficient, pre and post, lies on one line through the reference period. Read it beside the joint pre-trend test. If the joint test rejects and the adversarial test does not, the pre-period coefficients show a clean linear trend that could, by itself, account for the post-treatment estimates.

findings_all.quote: g = svsolve(M, z)
findings_all.what_is_wrong: In the primary adversarial statistic (wooldid_advW, alt == 0), the coefficients are whitened only on the eigenvectors of V with positive eigenvalues (z = T*b). Any component of b in V's null space is silently dropped, and the numerator df becomes rank(V) - 1. The altmethod branch in the same function refuses such a b (line 16093: norm(resid) > tol returns missing). The comment in wooldid_advstat says the failure caution 'covers ... a residual outside the covariance's column space', but that is true only for alt == 1. The help (sthlp 572) says the test is cancelled 'when the event-study covariance is degenerate'. In fact the code runs at any positive rank, and does not caution the way pretrendpower() does on a rank-deficient block. On a partially rank-deficient e(V_es_*), the p-value therefore ignores the coordinates the covariance calls exact, which biases it toward non-rejection without a word. The probe designs were full rank, so how often this happens in practice is unmeasured.
findings_all.correct_statement: When the event-study covariance is rank-deficient, a Wald-type line test should either decline or disclose that it tests only the retained subspace, as pretrendpower() does. It should not silently project the coefficients.

Either choice adds or changes a message, so it needs the author's wording ruling.
findings_all.reference: Andrews (1987), 'Asymptotic results for generalized Wald tests', Econometric Theory 3(3): a generalized-inverse Wald statistic is chi-squared with rank(V) df only if the tested vector lies in V's column space with probability one.

findings_all.what_is_wrong: The poisson att is the estimand-weighted mean of cell-level differences in log conditional means (each cell's beta_it = ln(E[y(1)]/E[y(0)]) under ratio parallel trends). It is not the level-scale ATT that Wooldridge (2023) defines for the exponential-mean DiD. It is not the log of the ratio of averaged outcomes either: exp(att) is a weighted geometric-mean ratio. The documents never overclaim this. They say linear index (log) scale, and a grep for percent, proportional or log-point interpretations found none. The author chose this scale on purpose (BS-6), and it keeps the delta method complete because the absorbed effects cancel.
findings_all.correct_statement: Each poisson cell effect is a log ratio of expected outcomes, and exp(b)-1 is that cell's proportional effect. The aggregates average these log ratios with the estimand's weights, so they are not the log of a ratio of aggregated means.

finding.quote: reported treatment effects will not vary as a direct function of these controls; the effect of these controls are partialled out from the reported treatment effects.
finding.what_is_wrong: coarsecohortcontrols() is built at ado:1397 as i._i#i._t#(vars): every treated cell gets its own control slope, and the (0,0) reference cell slope acts as the pooled slope. The term is not keyed on targetflag, and margins toggles only targetflag, so the treated cell's own slope stays in the counterfactual. The reported cell effect is therefore beta_it, the treated-cell intercept at control value 0 (for a factor control, the effect in the base category), not the cell ATT beta_it + xbar_it*(s_it - s_ref). The estimate moves when a constant is added to the control. Probe p1 (tau = 1 + .5(x-5) + 2g, true ATT 2.00, i = onset cohort, fe(unit)): coarse(c.x) -0.526, coarse(c.x+100) -49.40, coarse(c.x-5) 1.92, coarse(i.g) 0.97 (the g=0 effect), interactivecontrols(x) 1.92 at both x and x+100, controls(x) 1.94. Probe p2 (constant effect 1.5): coarse(c.x) 1.435 vs coarse(c.x+100) 1.747, so even under homogeneous effects the estimate is an extrapolation to x=0 with noise scaling in |xbar|. The same defect makes the BJS paragraph (sthlp:1160-1165, 'closer to the spirit of BJS') and example 3 (sthlp:1186-1188) misleading, and guide:614 and guide:641 repeat 'partialled out'.
finding.correct_statement: With cell-specific control slopes and a pooled slope estimated on untreated rows, the cell effect under an imputation counterfactual is beta_it + xbar_it*(s_it - s_ref), the average over the cell of the fitted outcome minus the fitted outcome at the pooled slope. That quantity is invariant to shifting the control by a constant. Reference: Wooldridge (2025, Empirical Economics), covariates enter the cohort-by-time interactions centred at cohort means so that the dummy coefficient is ATT(g,t); Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024, Review of Economic Studies), Y(0) imputed with covariate coefficients from untreated observations; the general result that the coefficient on a dummy interacted with an uncentred covariate is the effect at covariate = 0 (Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, ch. 6.2).
finding.proposed_fix: Code, ado:1397 (and the same fix serves ccc_absorb, F1b): enter the controls once as pooled regressors, and give each treated cell a slope on the control centred at its weighted cell mean, built on a copy that is 0 on reference rows: regressors (vars) plus i._i#i._t#c.(vars_cellcentred). The column space is unchanged, so the fit is unchanged, but the cell intercept becomes ybar_it minus the fitted Y(0) at the pooled slope, which is the cell ATT; margins still reads it by toggling targetflag, the effect stays constant within the cell (cell collapse stays exact, gteffects' 'reproduces exactly' stays true). For factor controls centre each indicator column within the cell, or use the alternative spelling (vars) plus i._i#i._t#1.targetflag#(vars) (same column space; margins then removes intercept and slope together, but the effect then varies within the cell, so coarsecohortcontrols must join fcbad at validate ~5872 and gteffects must add the slope term). Help, replace sthlp:845-850 with: {phang}{opt coarse:cohortcontrols()}: Includes the specified controls, and interactions between them and every Tz_it dummy in the model, one per cohort-time period for which a treatment effect is estimated (under {it:esfixedbaseperiod}, every estimable treated cohort by relative time period). The control slopes in the reference period and the control group are pooled, while each treated cohort-period gets its own slope. Each reported effect is the cell's average outcome less its predicted untreated outcome at the pooled slope, so it does not depend on where the control is centred. All coarse cohort controls must use factor notation, {it:c.} for continuous and {it:i.} for categorical. {p_end}. Guide:614 and 616, third column: 'partialled out at the pooled slope; the effect is the cell average'. Until the code is fixed, the help must say the reported effect is the treated-cell intercept at a control value of zero and that controls must be centred on their treated cell means.
finding.reference: Wooldridge (2025) Empirical Economics, covariate section; Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024) REStud; Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics ch. 6.2
finding.ruling_checked: Grepped review_process/ for coarsecohortcontrols, 'coarse cohort control', coarsecontrol, centr|center|demean with control, x=0|at zero|base category|location|units of. No ruling on the estimand. review_process/blue_sky_2026-09-18/repro/agents/nofastcollapse/NOTES.md:35 observes 'coarsecohortcontrols() expands to i._i#i._t#(x) - NOT interacted with targetflag - so it cancels' as a convenience for the collapse; never ruled as an estimand question.

verdict.reason: The finding holds up. ado:1397 builds coarsecohortcontrols() as i._i#i._t#(vars) with no targetflag. review_process/cell_collapse_followup_2026-09-01.md section (d) confirms that this term is the same at targetflag=1 and targetflag=0, so it drops out of the margins contrast. Each treated cell has its own intercept and its own slope on the uncentred control. The number wooldid reports is therefore the cell intercept at control = 0, and for an i. control it is the effect in the base level. It is not the cell ATT. That means the reported ATT changes when a constant is added to the control. It changes when the control is rescaled (for example Celsius to Fahrenheit). For i. controls it depends on which level is the base. Under homogeneous effects the estimate stays unbiased, but its noise grows with the distance of the cell mean from 0. The help says "the effect of these controls are partialled out" (sthlp:847). Guide 614, 616 and 641 say the same, and a reader will take that to mean the reported effect is the cell's average effect net of the control. It is not. The BJS paragraph (sthlp:1160-1165) and example 3 inherit the problem. Example 3's i.categoricalcontrolvar reports only the base-category effect. I found no author ruling on the estimand in review_process/. The only related records are the collapse note that the term cancels and ccc_absorb rulings about crashes and the ES window. The kind (CODE_ECONOMETRIC_ERROR) and severity (high) are right. The proposed fix is sound, and I checked numerically that it gives the same estimate after a shift. One claim should be softened. The centred spelling is close to the untreated-only imputation estimate but not identical to it (1.92997 vs 1.93019 in my probe). The reason is that within-cell unit variation in treated rows still informs the unit FEs and the pooled slope. So the help should not claim did_imputation equivalence.

N6 confirms that each subgroup estimate matches a run on that subgroup's subsample alone. si7 item 1 is about a crash. Neither looks at cell weighting.

The algebra: under the default att, subgroup g averages its cells tau_cgt with weights n_cgt/N_g. With i set to onset cohort by group and fe(i.g##i.t), the regression fits every cell separately, so tau_cgt = delta_cgt + s_ct, where s_ct is the cohort-by-period shock that hits both groups. The shock term in the contrast is sum (n_1ct/N_1 - n_0ct/N_0) s_ct. It is zero only when the group shares are the same in every treated cell. att_it gives equal weight to each (i,t) cell. When both groups cover the same cohort-by-period cells, its contrast is the equally weighted mean of the cell-level triple differences, so the shared shocks drop out.

Under the help's own definition ("difference in the diff-in-diff estimates"), the last sentence is true as a matter of definition. Under staggered adoption with group shares that differ by cohort, which is the usual case, it is not.

On the citations: Ortiz-Villavicencio and Sant'Anna's "not a difference of two DiDs" result is mainly about covariates and about pooling not-yet-treated comparisons. The aggregation point here follows from the algebra alone, so the help text does not need to cite them.

finding.quote: A cluster() strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells, bootstrap() or permute() gives valid cell inference.
finding.what_is_wrong: When a treated cohort-by-period cell lies wholly inside one cluster, a cluster bootstrap cannot recover that cell's own sampling variance. A cell that sits in one cluster is resampled whole or not at all, so its idiosyncratic noise never varies across replications. Only the control-side noise does. The bootstrap cell standard error is therefore understated for exactly the cells the caution counts, just as the analytic one is. Probe p1 used 30 units with a unit-level i, cluster(unit), 10 treated units, iid N(0,1) errors and no effect. The theoretical sd of a cell estimate is 1.12. The bootstrap(standard) reps(200) cell standard errors were .19 to .32, and several null cells printed p = 0. The analytic cell standard errors were .22 to .34. The att row is fine under the bootstrap: .249 against a Monte Carlo sd of .257, because the resampling does vary across treated units. The caution also prints inside the bootstrap run itself (log line 65), where it claims that the run just made gives valid cell inference. The permute() half is false by the help's own account: help L441-442 and L909 say the gteffects cells carry no inference under permute(). The same claim appears in help L316 (the remedies list covers the gteffects cells), help L909 ('under bootstrap() the cell inference is bootstrap-based', which implies it is valid), guide L200 (rule 2: 'gteffects cells are understated (cautioned). Use bootstrap() ... or permute()') and guide L214.
finding.correct_statement: Whether the variance is analytic or from resampling, a parameter identified from a single cluster's data has a variance that no cluster-level procedure can estimate. The cluster's own noise enters the estimate once and is never re-drawn. Only a cluster() strictly finer than the cell, so that several independent units lie inside each cell, gives valid cell inference. bootstrap() is valid for the aggregate rows, which average over many treated clusters. It is not valid for single contained cells. permute() posts no cell inference at all.

finding.quote: it protects only when the cluster-robust standard error is informative about the treated clusters - many observations per treated cohort-period cell, with `cluster()` coarser than the cell.
finding.what_is_wrong: The text gives the wrong condition for permtstat to protect. The regression carries a dummy for each treated cohort-by-period cell, so the OLS residuals in each treated cell sum to exactly zero. When a single cluster contains the whole cell, that cluster's score on the cell dummy is this zero sum. So the cluster-robust variance cannot see the cell's own error variance, however many observations the cell holds. A cluster 'coarser than the cell' is exactly the failing case. The SE sees the treated cells' variance only when each treated cell spans several clusters, that is, with cluster() strictly finer than the cell. The repo says this itself in three places: guide ch.4 ('cluster below the level of i ... so that every treated cohort-by-period cell contains several clusters'), the jtcoarse caution (it calls the covariance degenerate when i is nested in the cluster), and the permonsetcohorts entry ('A finer cluster() is also what makes permtstat protective'). The consequence goes further than the text admits. Without permonsetcohorts, permute() requires cluster() to nest i, so every treated cell lies inside one cluster and permtstat can never protect. It can protect only under permonsetcohorts with several clusters per treated cohort-period cell. The same wrong condition appears in the runtime caution at ado:6948 (listed in ch.14 at guide:984). Help:465 and guide:372 name only 'cluster() equal to i', and the caution fires only when clus == ivar. A cluster strictly coarser than i, such as i = unit with cluster(state), which is the classic few-treated-states layout, fails in the same way but gets no caution. A reader following the text would believe a size remedy is in force when it structurally cannot be.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds. Every treated i-by-t cell has its own dummy, and all the other regressors that touch the cell are constant inside it. So when one cluster holds the whole cell, the cell adds exactly zero to that cluster's score, however many observations it has. A cluster() "coarser than the cell" is therefore the blind case, not the protective one.

I ran a probe with 10 observations per treated cell, i = state and cluster(state). Scaling the treated cells' within-cell spread by 10 left the SE unchanged to six digits. Under cluster(unit), which is finer than the cell, the same change raised the SE about elevenfold.

The guide contradicts itself on this point. Guide 214 and the permonsetcohorts entry both say a finer cluster() is what makes permtstat protective. The runtime caution (ado 6948, listed at guide 984) makes the same mistake as guide 383: it blames only "one observation per i-period", so a user with many observations per cell and cluster() at i is told, wrongly, that they are protected.

finding.what_is_wrong: When some treated cohort-period cells have no within-cell dose variation (their dose slope is dropped for collinearity) but others do, the dropped slopes enter margins dydx(contreat) as exact zeros that keep their full weight. The void screen fires only when every treated slope is dropped. finding.correct_statement: A treated cell whose dose slope is not identified has no ame. finding.quote: When specified, {it:wooldid} will still present ATT-type average treatment effects estimates, which in this case should essentially be the integral of the estimated average marginal effects across the distribution of the continuous treatment variable.
finding.what_is_wrong: Under contreatwithin the att is a mixture, and the event study steps down mechanically at the last onset. In periods that still hold a not-yet-treated unit, the cohort-period intercept is identified and the att carries the full level effect of treatment. In periods where every unit is treated, the intercepts are collinear with the time effects. contreatwithin rewrites the working safety to off, so the dropped-dummy screen is skipped, one intercept per period is normalised to zero without a message, and only there does the att reduce to the dose-slope integral (relative to an arbitrarily chosen cohort). Measured (probe p4): onsets at t=3 and t=5, no never-treated units, true effect 1 + d (mean d 2.03, so true att 3.03 and slope integral 2.03). Reported att 2.366. ES post0 2.545 = one half of (3.03 + 2.03), because the onset-3 cohorts still have a not-yet-treated comparison at t=3 but the onset-5 cohorts have none at t=5. post2 = 2.023, the pure slope integral. The result is a spurious decline across horizons, and no caution prints. Relabelling the cohorts moves the att (2.366 to 2.368), which shows the normalisation depends on the solver. Even where every intercept is removed (for example i-by-t effects in fe()), the att is a linear extrapolation of the dose response down to dose zero, and it assumes that dose zero means untreated. The same sentence is at guide 603.
finding.correct_statement: Without an untreated comparison, the level effect of treatment in a cohort-period cell is identified only while some unit is still untreated in that period. Where no unit is, the cell intercepts are not identified and wooldid sets them to zero. The att there is only the dose part, the effect of moving from dose zero to the observed dose, extrapolated along the fitted slope. The reported att and its event study therefore mix the two kinds of period, and they can change sharply at the last onset for that reason alone. The ame does not depend on this and is the quantity to read.
finding.proposed_fix: Help 817-818 (and guide 603 in Markdown), replace the sentence with: When specified, {it:wooldid} still reports att estimates, but read them with care. The level effect of treatment in a cohort-period cell is identified only while some unit is untreated in that period. Where every unit is treated, the cell intercepts are not identified, and {it:wooldid} sets them to zero without a message. The att there is only the effect of moving from a dose of zero to the observed dose, extrapolated along the estimated slope. The reported att and its event study mix these two kinds of period, and can drop at the last onset for that reason alone. Rely on the ame results under {it:contreatwithin}. Optionally (author's call, new-message rule applies): count the treated cell dummies dropped under contreatwithin in wooldid_ccscreen (whose dropped-dummy loop is skipped when sw is off, wooldid.ado:13372) and print one caution naming the affected periods.

verdict.reason: The finding holds, and my own probe shows the problem is worse than the reviewer measured. The reviewer's proposed wording is itself wrong and needs correcting. Under contreatwithin, wooldid turns off two checks. It keeps calendar periods where every unit is treated (the calendar-support screen is skipped, ado:13703-13704). It also skips the scan for dropped treated dummies, because the working safety value is set to off (ado:5654, ado:13372). In a period with no reference rows, the cohort-by-period dummies add up to the time dummy. The solver then silently sets one cell's intercept to zero and measures the other cells in that period against it. The att in those periods is not the integral of the ame. It is the dose part plus each cohort's level effect minus the level effect of whichever cell was dropped. The reviewer's homogeneous-effect probe (p4) hides this, because there all those differences are zero. My probe gives cohort i a level effect of i, with a slope of 1. The true att is 4.13 and the dose part is 1.97. With the original cohort labels, wooldid reports att 1.472 and ES post2 = -0.591, which has the wrong sign. With the cohorts relabelled on the same data, it reports att 3.304 and post2 2.399. The ame is 1.001 in both runs, and no caution prints. An espre() window also takes pre-onset rows out of the reference pool. So a period can lose identification before the last onset: pre1 att moves from -0.0004 to -0.496 across the two labellings, which damages the pretrend reading. The help sentence is roughly right only when fe() absorbs every cohort-period intercept, for example with i-t fixed effects. That is the case the author intends (ado:13483, 'partial out any level effect'). Even then, the att extrapolates the fitted slope down to dose zero. The reviewer's correct_statement and proposed_fix say that in all-treated periods the att is 'only the dose part'. My probe refutes that, so the fix is corrected below. I found no author ruling on this sentence. Relaxing the checks is deliberate, but what the help says the att then equals was never ruled. verdict.reason:
The finding holds. The help (sthlp:1151-1155) and the guide's ch.15 table row give the conditions under which wooldid matches did_imputation with no controls, and they never say what level i must be. BJS is the unit-FE TWFE with every treated observation saturated, and that equivalence holds on unbalanced panels. With a coarse i, wooldid uses i dummies instead. By FWL the two agree only when the regressors, which are functions of (i,t), have the same unit means for every unit in an i. That is true when every unit in an i is observed in the same periods. Adding fe(unit) to a coarse i does not restore the match, because the cell-level treated dummies let treated rows inform the unit effects.

The reviewer's proposed wording is too strong. My probe shows that a panel which is unbalanced overall but balanced within each i matches exactly. So the condition is balance within i, not full balance, and the wording should say "observed in the same periods" rather than "balanced".

The project's own oracle test (test/suite/newfeat/bjs_identity.do) only checks the one-observation-per-i-t-cell case, which is i = unit. Severity medium is right, since users routinely set i to the onset cohort. The kind is closer to an omission, but DOC_MISDESCRIBES_CODE is acceptable.

finding.quote: 3. **`robust`** is appropriate when errors are independent across observations, which is rare in a panel; it does not carry the cell-containment problem, and the analytic `ame` standard errors are identified under it.
finding.what_is_wrong: With a unit-level i on a unit-by-period panel, each treated cell is one observation with leverage 1. Its own dummy drives its residual to exactly zero, so the heteroskedasticity-robust meat omits that observation's noise and the att standard error is understated. This is the same blind spot as cell containment. The code already treats it that way: ado 2366-2375 counts one-row cells under robust as contained, and the gteffects caution fires. Help L907 and L992 say so as well. The guide's decision rule contradicts both. Probe p2 on the p1 design gave a robust att se of .212 against a Monte Carlo sd of .257, 0.82 of the truth. The pre-pare-down help (62b121c) measured 0.64 and 70% coverage for a cell. Guide L105 repeats the error where it matters most, in the paragraph on when a fine i is right: 'Even then, prefer `robust` or a `cluster()` finer than the cell for the analytic run'. With one row per unit-period no cluster finer than the cell exists, and robust has the same defect.
finding.correct_statement: Under robust a treated cell holding a single observation contributes a zero residual, so its variance is missing from the sandwich and the standard errors are understated. robust avoids this only when every treated cell holds several observations.

verdict.reason: The finding holds. Guide L95 says to cluster "at the unit level or at any level strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells". Taken literally, "any level" covers unit-by-period clustering, which on a panel with one row per unit per period is the same as robust. It also covers clustering below the level at which treatment is assigned. Both are anti-conservative: Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan (2004) show this for serial correlation, and Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2023) show it for clustered assignment. Being finer than the cells is a necessary condition. It lets the analytic covariance see inside a cell, and it is what the containment mechanism needs. It is not sufficient for valid inference, yet the guide at L95 and rule 1 (L199), and the help's remedy list at L316, present it as though it were. The same gap sits in the help's other remedy lists (L561, L662, L826). Neither the guide nor the help says anywhere that clusters must be at or above the assignment level, or that they must keep a unit's periods together. The help's cluster() entry (L248) gives no guidance on level at all. The author has not ruled against this. SI-A1 (review_process/open_defects.md:301, 2026-09-10) only rules that clustering below i is the intended practice, and this finding leaves that intact. The ado comment at 7436 ("cluster() is a claim about dependence and assignment") shows the author holds the view the docs leave out. The blue-sky 09-18 items on finer clusters are about how the joint tests are calibrated, which is a different issue. The proposed fix is sound but can be improved. Its L95 wording drops "or coarser", which is valid and conservative. It never mentions serial dependence across a unit's periods. And it patches only L316, where the rule belongs once in the general cluster() entry. The help L316 part is closer to an omission than an error, since it is a remedy list for the containment mechanism. The guide L95 "any level" wording is a real misstatement, so medium severity stands.

finding.quote: Intuitively, this ought to be true whenever samples are large enough that sampling variation in covariates is ignorable (more precisely, ignorable within cohort-time period cells).
finding.what_is_wrong: The gap between conditional and unconditional standard errors does not shrink with sample size. Both variances are O(1/N). The extra unconditional term is the variance, across the treated sample, of the unit-level effect implied by the covariates and cell membership, scaled by 1/N. It is large whenever treatment effects are heterogeneous across cells or covariate values, and zero only when they are homogeneous. Probe p2 used two treated cohorts with effects 0 and 4 and unit clusters. The unconditional-to-conditional se ratio was 2.23 at 60 units and 2.29 at 600 units. The same misconception is in guide L307, which copies the paragraph, and in guide L202 (rule 4: 'when sampling variation in covariates or in the dose matters (small samples, influential weights)').
finding.correct_statement: Conditional (delta-method) standard errors are for the effect averaged over the treated units actually in the sample. Unconditional standard errors are for the population average. The two differ by a term that reflects heterogeneity of the effect across cells and covariate values. That term does not vanish as the sample grows, so the choice depends on the estimand and on effect heterogeneity, not on sample size.
finding.reference: Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2020), 'Sampling-Based versus Design-Based Uncertainty in Regression Analysis', Econometrica 88(1):265-296; Imbens (2004), 'Nonparametric Estimation of Average Treatment Effects under Exogeneity: A Review', Review of Economics and Statistics 86(1):4-29, sec. on population versus sample average effects.

Wooldridge (2025) expresses the view that conditional and unconditional standard errors often should be similar. They are similar when treatment effects vary little across cohort-period cells and covariate values. Where effects are heterogeneous the unconditional standard errors are larger, and the gap does not shrink as the sample grows: the conditional standard errors describe the effect averaged over the sampled treated units, the unconditional ones the population average. Sample weights that make particular observations very influential widen the gap further.' Keep the rest of the paragraph. Mirror the change in guide L307. verdict.reason: The finding holds. By default wooldid averages the implied unit-level effects over the treated observations and takes cell membership, covariates and dose as fixed (delta method). That standard error covers the sample-average effect. The margins vce(unconditional) standard error adds Var over treated units of the implied effect, divided by N (the SATE versus PATE distinction; Imbens 2004; Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge 2020). Both terms are O(1/N), so their ratio depends on how heterogeneous the effect is relative to outcome noise, not on sample size. The parenthetical "ignorable within cohort-time period cells" does not rescue the claim. Within a cell the extra term is Var(x'gamma_gt)/N_gt, the same order as the conditional term. The help's companion clause ("more impactful ... when samples are small") is wrong for the same reason. The finder's probe compares like with like: the same unit-FE model (fe(unit) nofastcollapse against controls(i.unit) unconditionalse), cluster(unit) finer than i, and two cohorts with effects 0 and 4. The ratio is flat in N, as theory predicts. No author ruling covers this paragraph. The only unconditional-SE rulings in review_process concern regress's (N-1)/(N-K) small-sample factor (change_audit_2026-09-22 round2), which is a separate issue. The proposed fix needs three changes. (1) Drop "widen the gap further" and keep the author's own hedged weights clause. It is his claim, and nothing here contradicts it. Influential weights scale both terms through the effective sample size unless the weights are correlated with the heterogeneity. (2) Keep the dose in guide rule 4. Under contreat() the ame rows depend on the observed dose values, which unconditionalse treats as random. (3) Split the long sentences to match the file's voice. Kind (DOC_ECONOMETRIC_ERROR) and severity (medium) are correct as filed.

unrefuted.quote: Randomization inference assumes clusters are exchangeable in **assignment** and fails when onset is systematically related to the outcome path - which is the identifying assumption the design already needs.
unrefuted.what_is_wrong: The text says randomization inference needs nothing beyond the DiD identifying assumption. That is false. Random (exchangeable) assignment of onset is strictly stronger than parallel trends: random timing implies parallel trends, but parallel trends does not imply exchangeable assignment. In the model-based reading, where assignment is fixed and errors are random, the test also needs the treated clusters' errors to be distributed like the controls'. It fails when the treated clusters differ in size or variance even though parallel trends holds. The guide's own ch.6 (line 383) says exactly this. So does the author's ruling the paragraph was drawn from: rulings_2026-09-07.md says RI 'fails when treated clusters are heterogeneous in variance'. The guide paragraph therefore misstates the ruling, and it invites a reader to treat belief in parallel trends as sufficient for valid RI.
unrefuted.correct_statement: Randomization inference is exact for the sharp null when onset was randomly (exchangeably) assigned across clusters. That assumption is stronger than parallel trends. When assignment is instead treated as fixed, validity needs the treated clusters to be exchangeable with the controls in their error distribution, and the test is mis-sized when they differ in size or variance even if parallel trends holds.
unrefuted.proposed_fix: Replace the quoted sentence with: "Randomization inference assumes onset was assigned exchangeably across clusters. That is stronger than parallel trends, which the design already needs. It fails when the treated clusters differ systematically from the controls in size or error variance, even when parallel trends holds (MacKinnon and Webb 2020)."
unrefuted.reference: Athey and Imbens (2022, J. Econometrics 226(1), 'Design-based analysis in difference-in-differences settings with staggered adoption'); Roth and Sant'Anna (2023, JPE Microeconomics, 'Efficient estimation for staggered rollout designs'), where random timing implies parallel trends but not conversely; MacKinnon and Webb (2020, J. Econometrics 218(2)).
unrefuted.ruling_checked: grep 'orthogonal' and 'exchangeab' in review_process/: rulings_2026-09-07.md:208 (the source of the paragraph) says RI 'fails when treated clusters are heterogeneous in variance', and research_2026-09-08/engine_parity.md:46 is the same. The ruled claim that the two assumptions are orthogonal and different stands. Only the clause equating RI's assumption with the identifying assumption departs from the ruling.

unrefuted.quote: A caution prints when fewer than 6 clusters are ever treated, since the set of distinct assignments is then small whatever {it:permreps()} is.
unrefuted.what_is_wrong: The counting claim is false in general. With k treated clusters at one onset among G clusters, the number of distinct assignments is C(G,k). For k = 5 that is 142,506 at G = 30 and 658,008 at G = 40. Sampled draws then almost never repeat, and the attainable p-values are not coarse. The advice the caution gives is also unavailable in exactly those cases, because permexact is refused above 65,534 assignments. The same claim is in guide:383 ('few ever-treated clusters means few distinct onset assignments, so sampled draws repeat ...') and in the runtime caution at ado:6972 (ch.14 guide:987). The caution fires on k < 6 without looking at the assignment count. The count M is computed later, in permrun, and the case of genuinely few assignments is already covered correctly by the 10-percent-of-M caution and the reported e(perm_npossible). With few treated clusters, the real concern is not resolution. It is that validity rests entirely on assignment exchangeability, and a handful of atypical treated clusters mis-sizes the test (MacKinnon and Webb 2020). So a user can be told their reference set is coarse when it has hundreds of thousands of elements, while the substantive few-treated risk goes unstated.
unrefuted.correct_statement: The number of distinct assignments is the product over strata of the multinomial coefficients, C(G,k) for one onset. It is small only when G is small or k is 1 or 2, and it is reported in e(perm_npossible). With few treated clusters, the reason for caution is that the test's size depends entirely on the treated clusters being exchangeable with the controls.
unrefuted.proposed_fix: Help 444: "A caution prints when fewer than 6 clusters are ever treated: with so few treated clusters the test's size rests entirely on their being exchangeable with the controls. The number of possible assignments is in {it:e(perm_npossible)}, and a separate caution prints when {it:permreps()} exceeds 10 percent of it." Guide 383: the same, in Markdown. unrefuted.quote: Romano and Wolf max-|studentized| step-down computed from the same replications, which controls the family-wise error rate across the horizons.
unrefuted.what_is_wrong: The code (wooldid_permstep, ado:18307) implements the step-down correctly, and it is exact under the global sharp null that no horizon of the family has any effect. That gives weak FWER control. An unqualified 'controls the family-wise error rate' reads as strong control: control over the true nulls whatever the other horizons are doing. Strong control is precisely what makes a step-down worth more than the single-step max-t. It requires subset pivotality: the null distribution of the true-null horizons must not depend on the false ones. Here it does. A reassigned onset carries the effect at one horizon into the null draws of the other horizons, which is the same mechanism the text itself describes for the pre-treatment rows. So under partial alternatives, control is not established. Guide:403 has the same problem: 'It is exact under the sharp null of no effect at any horizon of the family and controls the family-wise error rate across those horizons'.
unrefuted.correct_statement: The permutation step-down is exact, and controls the FWER, under the global sharp null of no effect at any horizon of the family (weak control). When some horizons have effects, reassigned onsets move those effects into the other horizons' null draws, so subset pivotality fails and strong control is not guaranteed.
unrefuted.proposed_fix: Help 483-484: "... computed from the same replications. It controls the family-wise error rate across the horizons when no horizon of the family has any effect. When some horizons do, the reassigned onsets carry their effects into the other horizons' null draws, so control over the remaining horizons is not guaranteed." Guide 403: replace 'It is exact under the sharp null of no effect at any horizon of the family and controls the family-wise error rate across those horizons' with 'It is exact under the sharp null of no effect at any horizon of the family, and under that null it controls the family-wise error rate across those horizons. When some horizons have effects, reassigned onsets carry them into the other horizons' null draws, so control over the rest is not guaranteed.'
unrefuted.reference: Westfall and Young (1993, Resampling-Based Multiple Testing, Wiley), subset pivotality as the condition for strong control; Romano and Wolf (2005, Econometrica 73(4), 'Exact and approximate stepdown methods for multiple hypothesis testing'), strong control under their monotonicity and null-distribution conditions.
unrefuted.ruling_checked: Searched review_process/ for 'strong control', 'weak control', 'family-wise' and 'step-down'. research_2026-09-08/engine_parity.md itself says 'A permutation step-down is exact under the global sharp null'. rulings_2026-09-07.md rules only that the step-down stays permutation-only. No ruling asserts strong control.

unrefuted.quote: It is not robust to the treated clusters being atypical in size or in error variance - relabelling then mixes clusters of different variance, and the reference distribution is narrower than the sampling distribution of the observed statistic (MacKinnon and Webb 2020).
unrefuted.what_is_wrong: The text states only one direction. MacKinnon and Webb (2020) find both: RI over-rejects when the treated clusters are small or noisy relative to the controls, because the reference distribution is then narrower than the sampling distribution, and it under-rejects when they are large, because the reference distribution is then wider. A reader whose treated clusters are large would conclude that the permutation p-values are too small, when they are too large.
unrefuted.correct_statement: When the treated clusters differ from the controls in size or error variance, the reference distribution and the sampling distribution of the observed statistic differ in spread. The test over-rejects when the treated clusters are smaller or noisier than the controls and under-rejects when they are larger or quieter.
unrefuted.proposed_fix: Replace the quoted clause with: "It is not robust to the treated clusters being atypical in size or in error variance. Relabelling then mixes clusters of different variance, so the reference distribution is narrower than the observed statistic's sampling distribution when the treated clusters are small or noisy, and the test over-rejects, and wider when they are large, and it under-rejects (MacKinnon and Webb 2020)."
unrefuted.reference: MacKinnon and Webb (2020, J. Econometrics 218(2), 'Randomization inference for difference-in-differences with few treated clusters'), simulations varying the treated clusters' share of observations.
unrefuted.ruling_checked: grep 'narrower than the sampling' and 'MacKinnon' in review_process/: no ruling on the direction. rulings_2026-09-07.md says only 'fails when treated clusters are heterogeneous in variance', which does not specify a direction.

unrefuted.quote: these different g() options set the reference effect of Contreat_jt relative to which Contreat_jt effects are estimated in treated cells.
unrefuted.what_is_wrong: The help and guide present the ame as 'the average marginal effect of the continuous treatment' and describe byTime as 'analogous to the second diff', but they never state the condition under which a within-cell slope across units has a causal reading. The ame is the slope, across treated units in the same cell, of the treatment effect in the dose, net of a reference slope. Parallel trends in untreated outcomes across dose levels identifies ATT(d|d) at each dose. It does not make the difference across doses a causal response. That also needs no selection on gains: higher-dose units must not have larger effects at every dose (the strong parallel trends assumption). Without it the ame equals the average causal response plus a selection-bias term. The same applies to the slope of the cfx att plot across dose bins. 'A bit speculative' (help 175) is a hedge, not the condition. The help's line 173 ('estimates of the effect of the continuous treatment variable can be computed within each treated i-t cell') and guide chapter 9 carry the same unqualified reading.
unrefuted.correct_statement: Under parallel trends in untreated outcomes across dose levels (given the chosen g()), the att at each dose is identified. The ame, and the differences in att across the cfx bins, measure the causal effect of more dose only under the stronger condition that units at different doses would have had the same treatment effects at any given dose. Otherwise they also carry selection bias from sorting into dose.
unrefuted.proposed_fix: Help, new paragraph after line 804: {pstd} What the ame measures. Within a treated cell, the ame compares units that received different doses. It is the causal effect of a marginal increase in the dose only if units at different doses would have followed the same path without treatment, and would also have gained the same from treatment at any given dose. The second condition is the strong parallel trends assumption of Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024). Without it, the ame also carries selection bias, since higher-dose units may simply be units with larger effects. The same holds for differences in att across the bins of the continuous treatment effects plots. {p_end} Guide chapter 9, decision rule 1, add: 'The ame is causal only under strong parallel trends (Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna 2024): units at different doses must share both untreated trends and treatment-effect functions.'
unrefuted.reference: Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024), 'Difference-in-Differences with a Continuous Treatment', NBER WP 32117 / arXiv 2107.02637, Theorems 3.1-3.3: standard parallel trends identifies ATT(d|d); comparisons across doses (ACRT) require strong parallel trends, else ACRT plus selection bias.
unrefuted.ruling_checked: grep -rni 'goodman-bacon|strong parallel|callaway|selection bias|ACRT|selection on gains' over review_process/ found only an unrelated blue-sky note on missing package comparisons (structure_and_ux.md:870). There is no ruling on the identifying assumption for the ame.

unrefuted.quote: the joint pre-trend and adversarial tests are not calibrated, the `ame` standard errors under `contreat()` are not identified, and the `gteffects` cells' intervals do not cover.
unrefuted.what_is_wrong: The bullet is about a unit-level i, where every treated cell holds one observation. There the ame POINT ESTIMATE is not identified. Every cell's dose slope is dropped, and the amevoid screen reports the whole ame family as missing (help contreat() entry). The cell-containment caution the sentence alludes to does not fire, because single-row cells are exempt (help 825, wooldid_amescreen detect: amerows >= 2). Saying only that the ame standard errors are not identified suggests the ame itself is usable in that design, and that finer clustering or the bootstrap would rescue it. They would not.
unrefuted.correct_statement: With a unit-level i, no treated cell has within-cell dose variation, so the ame itself is not identified; wooldid reports the ame results as missing, and no clustering or resampling choice changes that.
unrefuted.proposed_fix: Guide 92: replace 'the `ame` standard errors under `contreat()` are not identified' with 'under `contreat()` the `ame` itself is not identified, since a one-row cell has no dose variation, and wooldid reports it as missing'.
unrefuted.reference: A within-cell slope requires at least two distinct regressor values in the cell (rank condition).
unrefuted.code_site: wooldid_ccscreen amevoid wooldid.ado:13523-13544; wooldid_amescreen detect (amerows >= 2) wooldid.ado:14503-14507
